docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Web UI (React) --HTTP--> Server (FastAPI) --> Service layer <-- MCP server (AI agents)
 wireforge CLI / Python API -----------------> |-- Model (loader, validator, expressions)
                                               |-- Reference codec (Python)
                                               |-- Code generator --> C++17 or C99 code + test project
                                               |-- Wireshark dissector --> Lua plugin
                                               |-- Analysis (layout/ICD, trace, compatibility)
 Project files (YAML, git) <------------------ storage (files are the source of truth)

 Target software:  generated headers  +  runtime/include/wireforge/*.hpp
   Transport -> ring buffer -> FrameDecoder -> Dispatcher -> Receiver -> Handler::on<Message>Raw
                                                                  -> (default: decode) Handler::on<Message>Received
   Message struct -> serialize -> Encoder -> transmit buffer -> Transport

Implementation (Python package wireforge, codegen/wireforge/): loader, validate, expr (model); codec, golden (reference codec); generate, cpp*, test_project, test_cases (code and test generation); wireshark (Lua dissector plugin); layout, trace, compat, differential (analysis); fmt, service, cli (service layer and CLI); server/ (FastAPI), mcp_server (MCP), importers; resources locates the schemas, runtime headers, CMake package and UI shipped in the wheel. Web UI: ui/ (React, Vite). C++ runtime: runtime/include/wireforge/ (header-only).

docs.title: Boundaries
docs.text:
• The service layer is the single API; the CLI, the HTTP server and the MCP server are thin adapters, so every operation is available in all of them.
  • The runtime does not depend on the Python tooling; generated code depends only on the runtime (runtime/include/wireforge/ for C++17, .../wireforge/c/ for C99) and the standard library of its language.
  • Project layout: project.yaml and optional fragments (types/*.yaml, messages/*.yaml, interfaces/*.yaml, profiles/*.yaml) listed by include.

docs.title: Authoring
docs.text: Files are the source of truth. Two equal ways to work: the web editor reads and writes the project files through the server; or edit YAML in any editor (the JSON Schema gives completion and validation) and use the wireforge CLI or the Python API. The canonical formatter (wireforge fmt) keeps a stable key order and preserves comments, so GUI edits and hand edits produce clean git diffs. The server sees external file changes immediately and detects conflicting edits.

docs.title: Thread safety
docs.text:
• Generated serialize, deserialize and validate are pure and reentrant: no globals, no static mutable state.
  • Dispatch tables are const after initialization; registration happens before start() or is guarded by the lock policy.
  • Ring buffers: single-producer/single-consumer is lock-free; other topologies use a lock policy.
  • Link: the transmit path is serialized by the lock policy; poll() has a single consumer per link.
  • The default lock policy is std::mutex-based; it is a template parameter, so bare-metal and RTOS ports need no <mutex> (WIREFORGE_NO_STD_MUTEX, WIREFORGE_DEFAULT_LOCK).
  • ThreadSanitizer stress tests run in every gate run.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
• schema_version: file-format version; wireforge migrate upgrades files; the loader refuses unknown newer versions.
  • interface.version (semver): may appear in the wire header (role: protocol_version), in the generated banner and in the inline namespace, so several versions of an interface can coexist; wireforge compat reports breaking (layout, id, size, range), compatible and documentation-only changes and checks the version step.

docs.title: Portability
docs.text: Fixed-width types only; serialization by shifts and masks per byte (no reinterpret_cast, no packed structs, no unaligned access); no OS headers in the runtime; optional features behind configuration macros. Verified with GCC, Clang and MSVC, on 32- and 64-bit and little- and big-endian targets.

docs.title: Command line and Python API
docs.text:
pip install -e . installs the wireforge command. Every command is a thin front end of wireforge.service, which the server and the MCP server use as well, so every GUI or agent operation has a command line and a Python equivalent.

Command What it does wireforge init [dir] [--template telemetry\|command\|raw \| --protocol P] [--name N] [--namespace NS] [--version V] [--list] a new project from a working template or a published protocol (never overwrites; the directory must be empty) wireforge ci <project> [--base REV] [--test] [-o DIR] [--summary FILE] the check of a CI system: validate, compare with the project at a git revision (wire compatibility and version bump), optionally build and run the tests; one Markdown summary (docs/integration/github_actions.md) wireforge import-icd <file> <dir> --name N / wireforge import-dbc <file.dbc> <dir> --name N [--node NODE] [--skip-unsupported] a project from an ICD table, a C header or a CAN database (docs/IMPORT.md) wireforge import-mavlink <dialect.xml> <dir> --name N [--message NAME ...] a MAVLink 2 project from a MAVLink XML dialect and the files it includes (docs/IMPORT.md) wireforge validate <project> structural and semantic validation (file, line, JSON pointer per issue) wireforge fmt <project> [--check] canonical layout of every project file (comments kept) wireforge migrate <project> [--check] upgrade the file format and refresh the version stamps wireforge generate <project> -o <dir> [--tests] [--plugins F] [--language cpp\|c] C++17 code (or C99 with --language c, docs/CODEGEN.md), with --tests the GoogleTest project; custom checksums use --plugins F or else the project's plugins/*.py wireforge wireshark <project> -o <file>.lua Wireshark Lua dissector plugin (docs/WIRESHARK.md) wireforge analyze <project> [--profile P] [--format markdown\|csv\|json] layout report / ICD (docs/LAYOUT.md) wireforge compat <old> <new> [--interface I] interface compatibility and version bump check wireforge reqs-import <project> <file> --baseline B take a baseline of high-level requirements (ReqIF or CSV) as requirements/hlr_snapshot.yaml wireforge reqs-lock <project>, reqs-rename-key, reqs-list number the low-level requirements in llr_ids.lock, keep a number across a rename, list them (docs/DO178C.md) wireforge docs <project> -o <dir> [--strict] [--results <build>] [--export reqif,csv] [--source-url T] [--since REV] [--rule-findings FILE] requirements, design, test and traceability documents (docs/LIFECYCLE.md) wireforge trace <project> [--format markdown\|csv] [-o file] requirements, model elements, generated code and tests (docs/SAFETY.md) wireforge test <project> -o <dir> [--language cpp\|c] [--coverage] [--coverage-runtime] [--generator Ninja] generate, build and run the generated tests; the coverage build writes results/ for docs --results wireforge export <project> -o bundle.yaml / wireforge import <bundle> <dir> single-file bundles wireforge get <project> <pointer> value at a JSON pointer, e.g. /messages/NavSolution/fields/2 wireforge set <project> <pointer> <value> [--dry-run] [--strict] set a value (- as last index appends) wireforge upsert <project> <section> <name> <definition> create or update a type, message, interface, ... wireforge remove <project> <pointer> delete an element wireforge encode <project> <message> <value> [--interface I] [--profile P] payload (and frame) as hex wireforge decode <project> <hex> (--message M \| --interface I) decoded value (payload or frame), with the physical values of fields that have scale or offset

Values are YAML flow syntax (85, deg, '{ name: age, type: u8 }') or a YAML file (--file). --json prints {"ok", "issues", "data", "text"}. Exit codes: 0 success, 1 the project or check failed (validation errors, --check differences, insufficient version bump, test failures, codec errors), 2 usage error, 3 the command could not run (missing file or tool, invalid bundle).

docs.title: Editing keeps files diff-friendly
docs.text: set, upsert and remove find the file that defines the entry (root file or fragment; new entries go to the file that already holds that section, or to a new <directory>/<name>.yaml when the section keeps one entry per file) and edit it in place: comments, quoting, flow/block style and the order of named entries stay as written, updated entries keep the nodes (and comments) of unchanged parts, new mappings in a list of flow-style mappings are written in flow style. The file is then written in the canonical layout of wireforge fmt, so a hand edit, a GUI edit and another hand edit give a diff of exactly the changed lines (tests/python/test_cli.py::test_hand_gui_hand_edits_give_minimal_diffs). --dry-run returns the diff without writing; --strict refuses (rolls back) an edit whose result has validation errors.

docs.title: Canonical layout (wireforge fmt)
docs.text:
• keys of known mappings in schema order (project root, defaults, profiles, checksums, enums, types, messages, fields, occurs, checksum use, interfaces, framing, interface messages, user includes); user-named entries keep their order;
  • mappings indented by 2, sequences by 4 with the dash at 2, flow mappings written as { key: value };
  • comments move with the key they precede; a comment above the first key of a mapping stays at the top.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path
from wireforge import service

result = service.validate(Path("examples/01_basic_telemetry"))
assert result.ok, result.text
service.set_value(Path("my_project"), "/messages/Status/fields/0/max", 10)
report = service.analyze(Path("my_project"), export="json").data
wireforge.cli.run(["validate", "my_project"]) runs a command in-process and returns its exit code and JSON result.

docs.title: Generated C++ code
docs.text:
python -m wireforge.generate <project> -o <dir> [--tests] validates the project and writes, below <dir>/<project>/:

File Content user_prelude.hpp user_includes headers and prelude lines; static_asserts that application constants match the model (per profile via WIREFORGE_PROFILE_<name>) interfaces/<name>.hpp per interface, in namespace <ns>::<interface>::inline v<major>_<minor>: version constants, message ids and per-interface encodings, frame/buffer sizes, FrameFormat/HeaderLayout, Decoder/Dispatcher/Link types, Header, encode_frame(), decode_header(), Handler (on<Message>Raw, on<Message>Received), Receiver, Endpoint model.hpp define constants, checksum types, enums with is_valid(), types and messages, validate(), min_wire_size(), max_wire_size(), encode()/decode(), serialize()/deserialize()

Include directories: <dir>, runtime/include and the project's user_includes.include_dirs. Generated files are regenerated only when their content changes. The output does not depend on the profile: build a profile by passing its defines (-DPLATFORM_B=1 -DMAX_TRACKS=5 ...) and -DWIREFORGE_PROFILE_<name>.

docs.title: Data types (decision D28)
docs.text:
namespace demo::telemetry {
struct SensorReading {
    std::uint8_t sensorId{1U};
    SensorState state{SensorState::ready};
    float temperature{20.0F};
    Vec3 accel{};
    wireforge::StaticVector<std::uint16_t, 4U> samples;   // count field sampleCount is wire-only
};
constexpr wireforge::Status validate(const SensorReading& value) noexcept;
constexpr std::size_t min_wire_size(wireforge::TypeTag<SensorReading>) noexcept;
constexpr std::size_t max_wire_size(wireforge::TypeTag<SensorReading>) noexcept;
}
- Plain aggregates: SensorReading{} holds the model defaults. Each struct is documented with Defined in <file>:<line> (<JSON pointer>) and each member with its file:line (traceability, docs/SAFETY.md). A project with a requirements catalog adds Requirements: <HLR ids>; <LLR ids> to every struct, enum, checksum and interface; a project without one generates exactly the same code as before. - Fixed arrays are std::array<T, N>, counted or fill arrays wireforge::StaticVector<T, N> (an optional field is StaticVector<T, 1>), char arrays wireforge::FixedString<N>. - const, reserved, checksum fields and count fields used only as occurs.count: name exist only on the wire. - validate() checks min/max (also opaque user constants), enum membership, bit widths, element counts and nested values; it returns the first error. - Sizes are constexpr and follow the build's defines and #if blocks; call them as max_wire_size(wireforge::type_tag<SensorReading>).

docs.title: Requirement vectors
docs.text: With a vectors section the test project also has hlr_vector_test.cpp (TEST(HlrVector, <name>), one per profile a vector applies to) and the self-test checks the same vectors without a test framework. Each test decodes or encodes the vector's bytes and compares with the values written in the model, never with the reference codec, and records the requirement ids of the vector (docs/SCHEMA_SPEC.md section 18). A project without vectors gets neither file.

docs.title: User types
docs.text:
A user_types entry declares a field type WireForge never looks inside — only its fixed size_bytes: 

user_types:
  Fixed16:
    cpp: app::Fixed16
    size_bytes: 2
    include: app/fixed16.hpp
WireForge emits only the size query, into user_prelude.hpp: 
namespace wireforge {
constexpr std::size_t max_wire_size(TypeTag<app::Fixed16> /*tag*/) noexcept { return 2U; }
constexpr std::size_t min_wire_size(TypeTag<app::Fixed16> /*tag*/) noexcept { return 2U; }
} // namespace wireforge
The user writes the type itself (app/fixed16.hpp, included by user_prelude.hpp) plus its encode/decode, found by ADL exactly like a generated struct's: 
namespace app {
struct Fixed16 { std::int16_t raw{}; };
void encode(const Fixed16& value, wireforge::Encoder& encoder) noexcept {
    const auto bytes = std::bit_cast<std::array<std::uint8_t, 2U>>(value.raw);
    encoder.write_bytes(wireforge::Span<const std::uint8_t>(bytes));
}
void decode(Fixed16& value, wireforge::Decoder& decoder) noexcept {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 2U> bytes{};
    decoder.read_bytes(wireforge::Span<std::uint8_t>(bytes));
    value.raw = std::bit_cast<std::int16_t>(bytes);
}
}
A field of this type (occurs, arrays and nesting inside other types all work) is used exactly like a struct field; Encoder::write_bytes/Decoder::read_bytes (docs/RUNTIME.md) copy bytes onto/from the wire unchanged, leaving the type's own encoding entirely up to these two functions. Fixed16 must be default-constructible.

docs.title: C99 code (--language c)
docs.text:
wireforge generate <project> -o <dir> --language c writes <project>/model.h and <project>/model.c instead of the C++ headers; wireforge test ... --language c also writes, builds and runs a GoogleTest project that calls the C functions (the tests are C++, the code under test is C99), and the coverage target requires 100 % of the lines, branches and functions of model.c. The rules are those of the C++ code: the same layout on the wire, the same checks in the same order, the same statuses (wireforge/c/, docs/RUNTIME.md). What differs is the shape: - Everything global starts with the namespace of the project, :: replaced by _ (gnss::ubx gives gnss_ubx_): types <prefix>_<Type>, functions <prefix>_<Type>_init/validate/encode/decode, macros <prefix>_<NAME>. - An enum is an integer type with one macro per member (<prefix>_<Enum>_<member>) and <prefix>_<Enum>_is_valid(). - An array of variable size (a counted array, a fill array, an optional field, a string) has a member <name>_count next to the array <name>[capacity]; a fixed array has none. - <prefix>_<Type>_init() sets the defaults, _validate() returns the first error, a message has _serialize()/_deserialize() (its own encoding) and _serialize_with()/_deserialize_with() (an explicit wf_encoding). <prefix>_<Type>_MIN_WIRE_SIZE and _MAX_WIRE_SIZE are macros. - A checksum is the function <prefix>_checksum_<name>(data, length); a custom one calls the c_impl of the model. - A field with scale has <prefix>_physical_<Type>_<field>() and <prefix>_set_physical_<Type>_<field>(). - Each interface has <project>/interfaces/<interface>.h and .c, prefix <prefix>_<interface>_: the id and size macros (_HEADER_SIZE, _TRAILER_SIZE, _MAX_FRAME_SIZE, _<Message>_ID), _header and _header_init(), _encode_<Message>() (a complete frame), _decode_header(), a _handler struct of callbacks, _dispatch_frame() and a _link that owns its buffers (_link_init(), _link_poll(), _link_send_<Message>(), _link_send_frame()). A handler has, per message, on_<Message>_received (decoded) and on_<Message>_raw (the bytes before decoding; <prefix>_<interface>_<Message>_default_raw() decodes and forwards). A null callback means the default; a handler without callbacks ignores the messages. The link reads and writes through a wf_transport (two functions) and is used by one thread at a time (docs/RUNTIME.md). Only the types and enums that a message or an interface uses get functions. User types are not supported yet.

In CMake, wireforge_generate(<target> PROJECT <dir> LANGUAGE c) generates the C code at configure time and makes <target> a static C99 library of it, with the C runtime headers; it needs no C++ compiler, so it also builds for a microcontroller (examples/tutorial/drone_firmware).

docs.title: C++17 and C99 compared
docs.text: C++17 (default) C99 (--language c) Wire layout, checks, statuses, checksums, physical values yes the same rules Framing, dispatch, link over a transport (interfaces) yes yes Generated GoogleTest project, 100 % coverage gate yes yes (tests are C++, the code under test is C99) User types (user_types) yes no: generation stops with "user type X is not supported in generated C" Locks and atomics in the link yes no: a link belongs to one thread at a time (docs/RUNTIME.md) Generated by the command line, Python API, server and web UI yes yes; MCP generates C++ only CMake (wireforge_generate) yes yes, LANGUAGE c Wireshark dissector yes the same (it depends on the model, not on the language)

docs.title: Physical values
docs.text:
A field with scale and offset keeps its raw value in the struct (that is what the wire carries). Two functions next to the struct convert (SR-24 limits them to plain integer and floating-point fields): 

double celsius = physical_Climate_temperature(climate);        // raw * scale + offset
bool fits = set_physical_Climate_temperature(climate, 21.5);   // false, field unchanged, when the raw value does not fit
The setter rounds to the nearest raw value (halves away from zero) and refuses a value outside the range of the type or bit width, and NaN or infinity. min and max are not applied by the setter: they are checked by validate() and on encode, as for every field. The generated tests set both ends of the raw range through the setter, a value just below zero, values outside each end, and for floating-point fields a normal value and both infinities. The reference codec adds the physical values of the scaled fields to its decode result (physical).

docs.title: Codec
docs.text:
std::array<std::uint8_t, max_wire_size(wireforge::type_tag<SensorReading>)> buffer{};
std::size_t size = 0U;
wireforge::Status status = serialize(reading, wireforge::Span<std::uint8_t>(buffer), size);
status = deserialize(wireforge::Span<const std::uint8_t>(buffer.data(), size), reading);
- serialize/deserialize take an optional wireforge::Encoding (byte order, bit order, encode/decode range checks, trailing bytes); the default k<Message>Encoding uses the message and project settings. Interfaces pass their own encodings. - Per type, encode(const T&, wireforge::Encoder&) and decode(T&, wireforge::Decoder&) hold the field sequence. The encoder/decoder keep the first error, so the functions are straight-line code; statuses and their order match the reference codec (SPEC section 16). - Wire-only fields are produced by the encoder: consts, reserved values, checksums (checksums::<name> types) and count fields (from the array size); the decoder verifies them (ConstMismatch, ChecksumMismatch, count ranges). - Every golden vector is a test of the generated test project (see below): the C++ value built from the JSON value must encode to the golden payload, and the payload must decode and re-encode unchanged, for every profile.

docs.title: Interfaces
docs.text:
namespace node_c = demo::avionics::our_to_nodeC;   // inline namespace v1_0 holds the version
class App final : public node_c::Handler {
    void onCommandReceived(const demo::avionics::Command& command) noexcept override { /* ... */ }
};
App app;
node_c::Endpoint endpoint(app);                      // frame decoder + dispatcher + receiver
node_c::Link<MyTransport> link(transport, endpoint.decoder(), endpoint.dispatcher());
link.send([&](wireforge::Span<std::uint8_t> buffer, std::size_t& size) {
    return node_c::encode_frame(command, buffer, size, node_c::Header{/* seq */});
});
link.poll();                                         // calls app.onCommandReceived(...)
- Header fields with roles sync, message_id, payload_length, protocol_version and constants are written and checked automatically; other header fields are members of Header. A protocol_version field without const carries the interface major version. - Supported subset (D30): header fields are byte-aligned integers; the trailer holds at most one checksum plus constants; checksums in headers are not supported. Unsupported layouts are reported by wireforge.generate. A header bit-field is supported when it is unsigned, not a constant, a whole number of bytes wide and the header bit order follows its byte order (little with lsb_first, big with msb_first): each such field then has bytes of its own and is written with Encoder::write_width (a 24-bit message id after an 8-bit component id, as in MAVLink 2). - With trim_trailing_zeros the frame writer sends the payload without its trailing zero bytes (wireforge::trimmed_size, the first byte stays), and the default on<Message>Raw decodes the payload extended with zeros to the size of the message (wireforge::ZeroExtended); an override of on<Message>Raw gets the bytes as they were received. The generated tests add TrimsTrailingZeros (the frame of every default message has the trimmed size); the dispatch and golden tests send frames whose payloads were trimmed by the reference codec. - Every message has a virtual on<Message>Raw(const wireforge::RawMessage& raw) in Handler. Its default decodes raw.payload and calls on<Message>Received when the decode succeeds, and returns the decode status. Override it to take the bytes without decoding: framing, the frame checksum and the message id were checked, the payload was not (no size, constant, range or payload checksum check). raw.frame is the whole frame. Call Handler::on<Message>Raw(raw) from an override to get both. The spans point into the link's receive buffer and are valid only during the call.

class Relay final : public node_c::Handler {
    wireforge::Status onCommandRaw(const wireforge::RawMessage& raw) noexcept override {
        return forward(raw.frame);   // the frame as received, without decoding
    }
    void onCommandReceived(const demo::avionics::Command& /*command*/) noexcept override {}
};
- Both directions are generated for every interface (direction is documentation), so any interface can be looped back in tests. The golden tests encode every golden frame with encode_frame, compare it byte for byte and send it through a loopback Link to the generated Handler.

docs.title: Quality
docs.text: Generated code compiles with the full warning set (-Werror), passes clang-tidy, cppcheck and the GCC analyzer and is completely documented for doxygen. Snapshots of the generated examples live in tests/python/snapshots/; after an intended change run WIREFORGE_UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1 pytest tests/python/test_generate.py and review the diff. The generated code contains no branch that the generated tests cannot reach: checks that cannot fail are written with wireforge::status_if() and wireforge::size_if_ok() (runtime, D46). The generated tests cover every enum member and the decode errors and raw hooks of every message. The generated test project gates line, branch and function coverage of the generated headers; for the examples each is 100 %.

docs.title: Generated test project
docs.text:
python -m wireforge.generate <project> -o <dir> --tests [--plugins plugins.py] [--runtime runtime/include] [--coverage-threshold 100] also writes <dir>/<project>/generated_tests/, a standalone CMake project:

File Content CMakeLists.txt one GoogleTest executable per profile (profile defines + WIREFORGE_PROFILE_<name>), the quality-policy warning flags as errors, WIREFORGE_SANITIZE, WIREFORGE_CLANG_TIDY, WIREFORGE_COVERAGE with a coverage target (gcovr, fails below WIREFORGE_COVERAGE_MIN_LINE percent line coverage, or below 100 percent branch and function coverage (WIREFORGE_COVERAGE_MIN_BRANCH, WIREFORGE_COVERAGE_MIN_FUNCTION), of the generated headers) CMakePresets.json dev, asan-ubsan, tsan, coverage, clang-tidy .clang-tidy the repository's check set, warnings as errors golden_test.cpp golden vectors: payload round trip, encode_frame equals the golden frame, decode_header, loopback through Link/Endpoint/Handler message_test.cpp per message: defaults (T{}), every scalar member and the first element of every array at its minimum and maximum and one step outside (when the member type can hold it), an invalid enum value, every variable-size array emptied (the pattern value fills arrays to capacity), and single-byte mutations of the encoded pattern (the first one per distinct decode error and field: checksum, count above the maximum, constant, range), truncation and an extra byte interface_test.cpp per interface: every message dispatched to its handler, byte-wise delivery, bytes before the sync, a corrupted frame followed by a good one, encode_frame into too small buffers, raw delivery without decoding, raw delivery forwarded to the decoder, decode errors returned by the raw hook handlers.hpp, test_support.hpp, wire_support.hpp recording handlers with a loopback link per interface; assertion and byte helpers diff_harness.cpp <project>_diff[_<profile>]: line-based harness of the differential test (see below) selftest.cpp <project>_selftest[_<profile>] (CTest): framework-free self-test without exceptions, RTTI or heap (golden vectors: payload, frame, loopback; decode cases), for embedded and cross targets fuzz_target.cpp <project>_fuzz[_<profile>] (with -DWIREFORGE_FUZZ=ON, Clang): libFuzzer target; the first byte selects a message (deserialize, then a value that encodes must decode and encode to the same bytes) or an interface (bytes streamed in input-defined chunks through the loopback link)

Every expectation (payload bytes or the status) is computed by the reference codec (wireforge.test_cases), so the generated code is checked against the reference semantics; validate() must report the status the reference encoder reports with range checks forced on. Custom checksums need their Python plugin (--plugins) to compute expectations. After resynchronisation (resync: true without sync bytes, or sync bytes inside the corrupted frame) the number of rejected frames is not predictable byte by byte; the test then checks only that the corrupted frame is rejected.

The CMake paths to the runtime headers and the project's user_includes.include_dirs are relative to the test project when they share a directory with it, otherwise absolute; both are cache variables (WIREFORGE_RUNTIME_INCLUDE_DIR, WIREFORGE_MODEL_DIR). GoogleTest 1.14 is found or downloaded (FETCHCONTENT_SOURCE_DIR_GOOGLETEST reuses a local copy). In this repository tests/generated builds the test sources of every example with all gates (warnings, sanitizers, clang-tidy, cppcheck), and quality/run_generated_tests.sh builds each project standalone with its own CMake files and runs its coverage target (line, branch and function threshold 100 %, the default of --coverage-threshold; the examples and the models of tests/models/ reach 100 % in all three).

docs.title: Coverage of the generated code for any model
docs.text:
The 100 % gate of the generated headers is not shown on four examples alone; three checks stand behind it for every model a user can write: - quality/feature_matrix.py lists the features of the schema (every field type, bit-field form, occurrence form, header role, framing kind, checksum form, profile and condition) and fails when one is used by no built and measured model, or when a property of the schema is not mapped to a feature. The models are the examples, tests/models/ and the random models below. - quality/random_models.py writes valid random models (a fixed seed always gives the same model), generates their code and tests, builds them with the warning set as errors, runs them and measures the generated headers; any warning, failing test or coverage below 100 % of lines, branches and functions fails and leaves the model in build/random-models/failures/<seed>/. CI runs seeds 0 to 23 on every pull request and the workflow random-models-nightly runs 1000 more each night. A failure is a defect of the generator: fix it, reduce the model and add it to tests/models/. - SR-23: an enum field without a default needs a member with the value 0, because init() starts it at zero. - SR-24: scale and offset are allowed on plain integer and floating-point fields only.

A fourth check is made while the tests are written (wireforge.coverage_points): the model decides which points the tests must exercise (the frame writer of every message with too little room, the receiver check of every message, serialize without room, the decode error and the edit of every field, ...), every test records the points it covers, and a point that no test covers stops the generation with "defect of the generator". A generator that tests only the first message of an interface can no longer produce a project that misses the 100 % gate in a user's hands.

The checks found, and the generator now handles: the frame writer of every message of an interface (not only the first) is tried with too little room; a raw-decode error test uses the byte order of the interface; a message that is on no interface has a golden round trip of its own; serialize into a buffer without room is tested for every message; a message that exists only in some profiles is left out of the profiles without it; an unused pattern helper is no longer emitted. This is evidence over many models, not a proof; the user's own gate (coverage target, wireforge docs --strict) stays the last line.

docs.title: Results of a test run
docs.text:
The coverage target also writes machine-readable results to <build>/results/, which wireforge docs --results <build> turns into the test report, the resource document and the toolchain section (docs/LIFECYCLE.md):

On Windows the JUnit file of each test is named <suite>.<test>.xml; a path over 260 characters makes GoogleTest abort that test (exit code 0xc0000409), so keep the project and build directories short or enable long paths.

File Content junit/<executable>/*.xml GoogleTest result of every test, with the requirement ids it recorded ctest.xml CTest result, which includes the self-tests coverage.json, coverage_summary.json, coverage.cobertura.xml statement and branch coverage of the generated headers (gcovr; the Cobertura file is for other tools) coverage_runtime.json statement coverage of the runtime headers, only with WIREFORGE_COVERAGE_RUNTIME=ON toolchain.json compiler, CMake and gcovr versions, build type and the warning flags (no path)

WIREFORGE_COVERAGE_RUNTIME adds a second report for the runtime headers and fails below WIREFORGE_COVERAGE_RUNTIME_MIN_LINE percent of the statements (default 100). Only code that reaches the binary is counted, which is the code that flies; wireforge test --coverage-runtime sets the option. With coverage on, the tests are also built with -fstack-usage; the .su files next to the objects give the stack use of the generated and runtime functions. The coverage build is -O0, so these values are indicative; measure on the target.

A line the tests do not reach is either closed with a test or justified in an optional deviations.yaml in the project directory (not part of the model, no effect on the model hash):

schema_version: 1
deviations:
  - kind: coverage
    file: wireforge/ring_buffer.hpp          # runtime header relative to the include directory
    function: "wireforge::StaticSpscByteRing<*>::push"   # as gcov names it; * matches anything
    lines: [118, 119]                        # optional; absent: every uncovered line of the function
    category: defensive                      # deactivated | defensive | unreachable-by-design
    rationale: The ring cannot be full with this link.
    reviewer: J. Doe
A deviation with lines stops matching when a runtime update moves them, which makes the gap unjustified again so that the reason is reviewed. kind: rule entries are accepted by the schema and ignored for now.

docs.title: Differential and fuzz testing
docs.text:
python -m wireforge.differential <project> --harness <dir>/<project>_diff[_<profile>] [--profile P] [--plugins F] [--seed N] [--values N] [--mutations N] [--frames N] [--regressions DIR] sends inputs to the generated harness and compares every answer with the reference codec:

  • payloads (M <message> <hex>): random valid values of every message (every field random inside its range, random array lengths), the boundary and decode cases of the generated tests, and random mutations (replaced byte, flipped bit, truncation, appended bytes); the decode status, the status of encoding the decoded value again and the re-encoded bytes must be equal;
  • frames (F <interface> <hex>): random valid frames and their mutations through a loopback link; a frame the reference accepts must be dispatched with the same payload, a frame it rejects must not be dispatched cleanly (the stream decoder may split a rejected frame differently). Interfaces that resynchronise without sync bytes get only valid frames, and appended bytes are not used on framed interfaces (they start the next frame of a stream);
  • stored inputs in --regressions are replayed first and new mismatches are appended to found.txt there (tests/regressions/<project>/<profile or default>/).

--fuzz-seeds DIR writes the golden payloads and frames as seeds of the generated fuzz target. The random generator is a deterministic xorshift, so a seed reproduces a run. The runtime has its own fuzz targets (tests/fuzz/, preset fuzz): checksum_fuzz (table and bitwise CRC engines agree, split updates equal one-shot updates, six CRC variants) and frame_decoder_fuzz (three framings streamed in random chunks; every delivered frame is complete, has the sync value and a correct checksum, the ring always gets free space).

Gates: quality/run_generated_tests.sh runs the differential test for every example and profile; quality/run_fuzz.sh builds all fuzz targets with Clang and runs each for WIREFORGE_FUZZ_SECONDS (20 locally, 60 in CI, 900 in the weekly fuzz-long workflow, whose four jobs take every fourth target each through WIREFORGE_FUZZ_SHARD=k/4), WIREFORGE_FUZZ_JOBS targets at a time (default: the number of CPUs), seeded with tests/regressions/fuzz/<target>/ and the golden vectors; a crash leaves its input in build/fuzz/artifacts/.

docs.title: Coding rules: what is enforced and how
docs.text:
This document maps rule categories to the checks that enforce them in WireForge. It is an engineering coverage map, not a conformance claim. MISRA® and AUTOSAR® rule texts are copyrighted and not reproduced here.

WireForge's gating rule set is the baseline of docs/SAFETY.md: compiler warnings, clang-tidy, cppcheck, the compiler and Clang analyzers and the sanitizers (quality/run_all.sh). MISRA C++:2023 and AUTOSAR C++14 are not gates. Conformance to either needs a licensed checker and a deviation process; WireForge does not provide those. A user who has them runs their own tool on the generated code and the runtime and gives the findings to WireForge.

The reference is MISRA C++:2023, which absorbed most of AUTOSAR C++14. Rule numbers and texts are left out on purpose: the mapping below is at the level of topics, and every row marked to verify must be checked against your licensed copy before you rely on it.

docs.title: Advisory run with an open-source checker
docs.text: quality/run_misra.sh runs cppcheck's MISRA C:2012 addon as a rough proxy on C++ code (the open-source addon implements MISRA C, not MISRA C++ or AUTOSAR). It never fails a build and the CI job misra is not a required check. It reports the findings per rule and writes build/misra/findings.xml. Many C rules are meaningless on C++ (for example the single-exit and implicit-type rules), so read the result as a hint, not as coverage. Set WIREFORGE_MISRA_RULE_TEXTS to a rule text file you are licensed to use to get rule texts in the report; WireForge never stores one.

docs.title: How WireForge compares
docs.text:
WireForge is for one situation: the wire format is given (by an ICD, a standard, a device or the other team) and you need C++ or C code for it that does not allocate, plus evidence that the code does what the format says. The tools below solve neighbouring problems; several of them are the better choice when your situation is different.

Tool Who decides the wire format Generates Fits best when WireForge you describe an existing format, field by field C++17 or C99 encoders, decoders, validation, framing and dispatch; a GoogleTest project with coverage gates; a Wireshark dissector; layout reports and lifecycle documents the format is fixed by someone else, the target is embedded C or C++, and the code must be proven, not only written Protocol Buffers protobuf (tag, varint, length) many languages both ends are yours and you want schema evolution across languages nanopb protobuf C for microcontrollers, static allocation as protobuf, on small targets FlatBuffers, Cap'n Proto the library (zero-copy layout) many languages large messages read in place, both ends yours Kaitai Struct you describe an existing format parsers in many languages (serialization is limited) reading and exploring existing binary formats and files mavgen (MAVLink) MAVLink complete MAVLink libraries from the XML dialects you need message signing, the standard microservices or languages other than C and C++ cantools CAN databases (DBC) Python encoding and decoding, C source for signals CAN analysis and tooling in Python ASN.1 compilers ASN.1 encoding rules (BER, PER, ...) many languages the protocol is specified in ASN.1 Packed structs and memcpy the compiler nothing never for a wire format: byte order, alignment and padding differ between targets

docs.title: In more detail
docs.text:
Protocol Buffers, nanopb, FlatBuffers. These define their own encoding. They cannot express a format that someone else already fixed (a sync word, a 3-byte id, a CRC over the header and payload, bit-fields packed LSB first), and they are not meant to. If both ends are yours and you can choose the format, they are mature and well supported in many languages, which WireForge is not: it generates C++17 and C99 only.

Kaitai Struct is the closest in spirit: it also describes an existing format field by field, and it targets many languages. It focuses on parsing; WireForge generates both directions, the framing of a byte stream, the dispatch of messages to handlers, and the tests that check the generated code against an independent reference codec. Kaitai is the better tool for reverse engineering file formats and for languages other than C and C++.

mavgen and the official MAVLink libraries. They are the reference: message signing, the MAVLink microservices and many languages. WireForge reads the same XML dialects (wireforge import-mavlink common.xml, every message, checked byte for byte against pymavlink) and generates allocation-free C++17 or C99 with its own tests, coverage gates, a Wireshark dissector and traceability; it refuses signed frames. It fits when MAVLink is one of several protocols of a system that WireForge already describes, or when the generated code must come with evidence.

cantools imports CAN databases and encodes and decodes in Python. WireForge imports the same DBC files (wireforge import-dbc) and generates C or C++ for the target, with the same tests as any other model.

Hand-written code is how most of these links are implemented today. It works until a field moves, a target has a different byte order, or nobody remembers which side changed. The point of a model is that the code, the tests, the dissector and the documents change together, and wireforge compat tells whether a change breaks the other side.

docs.title: What WireForge does not do
docs.text:
• Languages other than C++17 and C99 (Python has the reference codec, not generated code).
  • Self-describing or schema-evolving encodings: there are no tags on the wire unless your format has them.
  • Encryption, authentication or message signing.
  • Production use without a commercial license (development, evaluation and CI are free; the generated code and its runtime are yours under MIT). See the README.

docs.title: Design decisions
docs.text:
The reasons behind the main design choices. Other documents refer to them by number.

# Topic Decision D1 Optional fields Unified with dynamic arrays as an occurrence model: every field has occurs {min,max}; optional = max 1, array = max N. Count comes from: a variable (any integer/bool field), an expression, or a constant. Count 0 = field absent on the wire. C++ repr: StaticVector<T,MAX>-like (count + storage), no heap. D2 Bits Bit-fields supported (bits: n, bool1, enums, nested groups). D3 Endian Message level only (interface may define default, message may override). No per-field endian. D4 Checksums Optional. CRC32 built in; parametric CRC engine; user-defined checksum via a documented C++ contract + schema reference. D5 Thread safety Runtime is thread-safe by design (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, Thread safety). Generated codec code is pure/reentrant. D6 Portability C++17 only, platform/compiler/endianness independent, no host-layout assumptions. D7 Versioning Two levels: schema_version (file format, with migrations) and interface.version (ICD semantic version, coexisting versions, compat checker). D8 Test generation Generator also emits a ready CMake project with GoogleTest tests and a coverage target. D9 Static analysis Zero warnings / errors / notes policy for runtime AND generated code (see quality/QUALITY_POLICY.md). D10 Bit order Selectable per message: bit_order: msb_first (default) or lsb_first. Applies to all bit-fields in that message; layout analyzer shows the effective bit map. D11 Floating point IEEE-754 only: f32 (binary32) and f64 (binary64), written/read via fixed-width integer bit patterns (memcpy), message-level endian. No scale/offset or fixed-point attributes in v1. D12 Static analysis rule set Baseline set only (compiler warnings + clang-tidy + cppcheck + analyzers + sanitizers). MISRA/AUTOSAR out of scope for v1. D13 Default lock policy StdMutexLock (std::mutex) is the default; NullLock and user-defined locks remain opt-in. D14 Server/tooling language Python for core, CLI, codegen, server (FastAPI), MCP (official Python SDK); TypeScript only for the UI. UI types are generated from the JSON Schema + OpenAPI so no logic is duplicated. D15 Authoring modes Files are the single source of truth. Everything is editable by GUI or by text/script: YAML files, wireforge CLI, Python API. GUI writes through the same canonical formatter, preserving comments and key order, so both modes coexist in git. D16 Checksum contract Static member functions only: kSize (1..8), State, init(), update(State&, Span<const uint8_t>), finalize(const State&) -> uint64_t, all noexcept; checked by is_checksum_v. The value is written with the message endianness. D17 Lock default without <mutex> WIREFORGE_DEFAULT_LOCK selects the default policy; otherwise StdMutexLock, or NullLock when WIREFORGE_NO_STD_MUTEX is set (bare-metal single-core default; RTOS ports set the macro). D18 Span conversions Every Span constructor is explicit, including Span<T> -> Span<const T>, so no analyzer suppression is needed (cppcheck noExplicitConstructor). D19 Bit-group container A bit group is packed into ONE container integer (8..64 bits, multiple of 8): msb_first gives the first field the most significant bits, lsb_first the least significant; the container is then written with the message endianness. Groups wider than 64 bits are not supported by the runtime. D20 Expression back ends One AST, three back ends: the Python evaluator wireforge.expr.evaluate (reference semantics, used directly by the tools and the reference codec, so no Python source is emitted), to_cpp (int64 C++ expression) and to_preprocessor (#if). Python is stricter than C++17 where C++ would be implementation-defined (shifting negative values): such models are rejected. Equality is proven by compiling truth tables with g++. D21 Validation variants Expressions are evaluated per profile when the project has profiles (profile defines override root defines), otherwise once with the root defines. Errors inside a profile are SR-16, otherwise SR-5. D22 Names in expressions Field names are allowed only in occurs.count (SR-7); min/max, capacities and sizes are static. In if: plain names must be root defines (always emitted as macros); profile-only macros are tested with defined(NAME); user constants (C++ symbols, not macros) are not allowed in if:. D23 Generated C++ name space Defines, enums, types, messages and interfaces share one generated C++ scope, so their names must be unique across these sections (SR-2); names that are C++ keywords or reserved identifiers (__x, _X) are rejected. Messages cannot be field types (shared layouts go to types). D24 Frame decoder Sync and length header fields are whole bytes in the frame byte order; the frame checksum is a trailer field. A rejected frame is reported once; resync: true skips one byte and rescans, resync: false drops all buffered bytes. Wrong sync bytes are skipped silently (counted). A frame larger than the ring capacity is InvalidLength. Framing none bypasses the decoder. D25 Transport interface The runtime defines a generic non-blocking transport (send/receive over spans, checked by is_transport_v, optional ITransport base) instead of depending on a particular driver API; existing drivers are connected through a small adapter class. D26 Compat classification Wire-level comparison per profile with three classes (breaking / compatible / doc) mapped to major / minor / patch, also for 0.x versions. Any range or enum value change is breaking (either peer may reject the other's values). Appended trailing fields are compatible only when the old interface allows trailing bytes. D27 Codec details Plain-name counts are written from the element count; expression counts must match. Fixed char arrays are zero padded and stripped on decode. Fixed framing never pads. Count overflow is reported as CountExceedsMax before the count field's own range. Custom checksums use plugins in Python (PLUGINS dict in a file next to the example). See SPEC section 16. D28 Generated C++ shape Types and messages are plain aggregates with default member initializers; validate(), min_wire_size()/max_wire_size() and the codec are free functions found through ADL (wireforge::type_tag<T> for size queries). Storage: fixed arrays std::array, counted/fill arrays StaticVector, char arrays FixedString. const, reserved, checksum fields and count fields referenced only as plain occurs.count names are wire-only (no member; the array size is the count). Defines become overridable constants, never macros. One generated tree serves every profile (#if blocks, define constants). D29 Generated codec Free serialize/deserialize per message with a runtime wireforge::Encoding argument (one code path for every interface); Encoder/Decoder with a sticky first error keep generated functions branch-free. NaN is outside every min/max range (reference codec and C++ agree). D30 Generated interfaces One header per interface in an inline version namespace (v<major>_<minor>). Handlers are virtual on<Message>Received(const M&) noexcept (no RTTI needed); Receiver decodes on the stack (reentrant) and Endpoint bundles decoder, dispatcher and receiver. Header fields must be byte-aligned integers and the trailer may hold one checksum plus constants; both directions are always generated. D31 Generated test project generate --tests writes a standalone CMake/GoogleTest project next to the generated code. Expectations are computed by the reference codec at generation time (no hand-written oracle in C++): golden vectors, boundary values, emptied arrays and single-byte decode mutations (first per distinct status and field). One executable per profile. Coverage is line coverage of the generated headers via gcovr (default threshold 90 %, repository gate 95 %); runtime headers are covered by the runtime tests. Unknown message ids are covered by the runtime dispatcher tests, not per interface. D32 Layout analyzer One analyzer for every profile; offsets are ranges after variable-size fields, element fields are shown for the first element, bit positions count from the container's least significant bit. The RAM budget counts the buffers the generated Link owns (receive ring, receive frame, transmit frame); buffers.tx_bytes sets kTxBufferBytes (checked to hold a frame) but the link's transmit buffer is one frame. Generated tests assert the analyzer's sizes against the generated constants. D33 Differential and fuzz testing The generated project contains a line-based harness (one process per profile, all inputs in one batch) instead of linking Python and C++; the reference codec computes every expectation. Rejected frames are compared only for "not dispatched cleanly" because a byte-stream decoder may consume a bad frame in other pieces than the one-frame reference. Findings: an unframed read longer than the frame buffer was split by Link::poll() and its first part dispatched; it is now InvalidLength and dropped. The reference codec keeps NaN bit patterns (WireNaN) so signaling NaNs round-trip bit-exactly like the C++ code. Fuzzing uses libFuzzer (Clang) with ASan/UBSan. D34 Portability matrix Cross builds use Debian/Ubuntu cross compilers (s390x big-endian, i686 32-bit) with qemu user emulation through CTest's emulator, so the same test suites (runtime, generated GoogleTest, self-tests) run on every target; locally the toolchains can be extracted without root (quality/fetch_cross_toolchains.sh). A generated framework-free selftest.cpp (golden vectors, decode cases) is built with -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti like embedded code. Platform-width conversions use narrow_to<T>() (a template, so 32-bit targets get no useless-cast warning). Clang -Weverything gates production code with four documented exclusions. D35 CLI, service layer and canonical format One service layer (wireforge.service) returns Result objects for the CLI, Python API, server and MCP. Edits address elements by JSON pointer, edit the defining file with ruamel round-trip and write the canonical layout; the canonical key order follows the schema but matches the hand-written examples (e.g. field units after the range), so formatting the examples is a no-op. Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 failed check, 2 usage, 3 cannot run. D36 Server storage No server-side cache or database: requests read the project files, so hand edits and git operations are visible at once. Optimistic locking with ETags (per file for file writes, per project for entry/value edits; 428 without If-Match, 412 when stale) and one write lock per project. External changes are announced by a long-poll endpoint instead of a file-system watcher (portable, no extra dependency). Auth is a shared bearer token or OIDC (D48). FastAPI/uvicorn are an optional extra (wireforge[server]). D37 Server tools generate returns a self-contained zip (generated code, test project, runtime, model copy) built in a temporary directory so every CMake path is relative inside the zip. Checksum plugins are found by convention in plugins/*.py (defining PLUGINS); the server therefore executes project code and serves trusted workspaces only. Compatibility compares two projects of the workspace (e.g. a released copy and the working copy). D38 UI stack React 18 + Vite + TypeScript strict; types generated from the JSON Schema and the OpenAPI document (checked in, verified by check:types), so the UI carries no hand-written model or API shapes. The server's result routes declare a ResultResponse model for that purpose. UI tests run against a real server process instead of mocks. Edits are saved explicitly (Save button) per entry, not on every keystroke. D39 MCP server Official Python SDK 2.x (MCPServer, stdio). The tools wrap the service layer like the CLI and the HTTP server, work on a workspace like the server, return the service Result as structured output and report bad arguments as tool errors. Besides the listed tools there are create_project, upsert_entry (all other sections) and run_tests, so an agent can go from an ICD to passing tests without leaving MCP. D40 Importers A documented one-row-per-field ICD table (CSV, or the first Excel sheet via optional openpyxl) and a C-header subset (fixed-width types, bit-fields, arrays, enums, integer defines) import into a new single-file project written in the canonical layout and validated at once; anything outside the subset is an error with file and line instead of a guess. Interfaces, framing and checksums are not part of the import. D41 Safety evidence The no-heap check inspects object files built like embedded code (no exceptions, no RTTI, no std::mutex, -O0 and -O2) with an allow list instead of a deny list. Findings fixed on the way: std::array::at (exception path) replaced by wireforge::array_at, virtual destructors of Handler/ITransport (deleting destructor referenced operator delete) made protected and non-virtual. Trace data comes from the model's source locations; generated code carries Defined in file:line comments. The coding-rule mapping is informative, not a conformance claim. D42 Packaging One wheel (pip install wireforge[server,mcp,import]) carries the JSON Schemas, runtime headers, CMake package and the built UI below wireforge/_data (copied by setup.py at build time; a checkout uses the repository files). The CMake package is hand-written and relocatable, so the same files work from cmake --install prefixes and from the wheel (wireforge cmake-dir); wireforge_generate() runs the generator at configure time and reconfigures when model files change. The Docker image adds the C++ toolchain and serves the UI. D43 License runtime/ is MIT licensed. Everything else (CLI, codegen, server, UI, MCP server) is Business Source License 1.1, free for non-production use and converting to MIT on 2036-10-17; production use requires a commercial license. Generated code is output of the tool from the user's model; WireForge claims no rights to it, and it only depends on the MIT-licensed runtime, so it carries no restriction.

| D44 | Wireshark dissector | One self-contained Lua plugin per project: a generated data table (every profile's layout, fields expanded per message so bit masks follow each message's bit order) plus a fixed interpreter that mirrors the reference codec, instead of generating Lua code per field. One protocol per interface; profiles are a protocol preference, so the ProtoFields are the union of all profiles. Fields of up to 4 bytes use Wireshark's own decoding (masks, sign extension, valuestrings); wider bit groups and 64-bit bounds use UInt64/Int64, so Lua 5.2 (doubles) and 5.4 behave the same. Only the 3.6 Lua API is used; bit operations come from bit32 or, on Lua 5.3+, native operators. The dissector reports every problem it finds, with the codec status as the expert text prefix. Plugins run in separate Lua environments, so custom checksums are hooks on _G.wireforge_checksums. Tests run real tshark 3.6, 4.2 and 4.6 against the reference codec, using packages fetched without root. | | D45 | Raw delivery | Whether a message is decoded is the consumer's choice, not part of the wire format, so it is not in the model and needs no setting. Every generated Handler has a virtual on<Message>Raw(const wireforge::RawMessage&) per message whose default decodes and calls on<Message>Received; the on<Message>Received stays pure virtual, so a forgotten message is still a compile error. MessageHandler and FallbackHandler receive the payload and the whole frame. The raw path does no size check; its spans are valid only during the call. | | D46 | Branch-free generated code | Generated code holds no branch of its own: a condition that the generator needs is written as a call to a runtime helper (status_if(), size_if_ok(), first_error()), and the runtime helpers are unit tested for both outcomes. The generated test project gates 100 % branch and function coverage of the generated headers next to the line gate. Checks that cannot fail after validation (for example that a frame fits max_frame_size, which SR-16 guarantees, or that attach fails, which SR-9 excludes) are kept as status expressions instead of being removed, so a future change that breaks the guarantee still reports an error. | | D47 | User types | A field type may be a user-owned, opaque C++ type: declared by size_bytes only, serialized by the user's own encode/decode free functions (ADL, same contract as generated structs, D28/D29); WireForge generates only min_wire_size/max_wire_size (both equal to size_bytes, since the size never varies). The reference codec and test generator never interpret the type's internal semantics: its Python-side value is raw bytes, generated tests skip per-field value assertions on it, and the Wireshark dissector shows it as raw hex (FT_BYTES). Occurs, nested structs and arrays all work (treated like a struct field for codegen purposes); bits, checksums, occurs.count, and min/max/default/const are rejected (already caught by existing rules, no new ones needed). |

| D48 | Server OIDC | wireforge serve --oidc-issuer URL --oidc-audience A verifies Authorization: Bearer <JWT> (signature from the issuer's JWKS found by discovery, iss, aud, exp/nbf with 60 s skew, asymmetric algorithms only) and is exclusive with --token (usage error, exit 2). The sub/email claims are kept on the request only, so the no-database rule of D36 holds. The JWKS is cached in memory and refetched lazily after --oidc-jwks-cache-seconds, without a background thread. Verification uses joserfc (authlib.jose is deprecated) in the optional extra oidc. Still no roles, per-project permissions or audit log: every authenticated user has the access of a token holder. | | D49 | Requirements and LLR | The user owns the high-level requirements (the requirements catalog); model elements point at them with reqs. Low-level requirements are derived from the model, never stored, and keyed by names (Owner[.field].KIND) so reordering fields keeps them and a rename changes them; the displayed id comes from one function. Fields of a nested type belong to the type, so a requirement is stated once. Generated tests, not naming conventions, carry the link: each records its LLR ids with RecordProperty and the trace report reads them from the test sources. The layout analyzer's static size assertions became WireSize tests so SIZE and FRAME_MAX have a real test; every interface gets FRAME_ENCODE, FRAME_MAX, DISPATCH and RAW, so no generated test lacks a requirement. The generator is not qualified: generated code is verified like hand-written code and WireForge produces the evidence. Defaults do not change: validate only checks references (SR-21), a project without a catalog generates the same code (only the format banner moves to 1.1), and the Requirements: Doxygen lines exist only with a catalog. Requirement ids are the user's data, so the rule that comments never cite decision numbers does not apply to them. DISPATCH_UNKNOWN is verified by the runtime tests (D31). RANGE, ENUM and BITS are derived only for the directions where range_check is on. | | D50 | Lifecycle documents | The documents come from one pure renderer (wireforge.lifecycle) over the model, the derived low-level requirements, the trace and the layout analysis, and the CLI, server and MCP only wrap it. The output is deterministic (no date, user name or absolute path) so it can be committed and diffed. The default run never fails because requirements are missing: --strict turns four review findings into an exit code, so existing projects keep working. Derived low-level requirements are reported, not rejected, because the standard allows them. The DO-178C table quotes no text, only objective numbers and our own wording, and rows we could not settle without the standard are marked check for the owner of the licensed copy. No output says certified or compliant; the generator stays unqualified and the files are evidence for the applicant's process. | | D51 | Coding-rule coverage | The baseline of D12 stays the only gating rule set. MISRA C++:2023 and AUTOSAR C++14 appear as a topic-level coverage map (docs/CODING_RULES.md) that quotes no rule text; rows we could not settle are marked for the owner of the licensed copy. cppcheck's open-source MISRA addon implements MISRA C:2012, so it runs only as an advisory proxy (quality/run_misra.sh, non-required CI job) and is never presented as MISRA C++ coverage. Conformance needs a licensed checker and a deviation process, which WireForge does not provide. | | D52 | HLR vectors as independent oracle | The reference codec and the generated C++ share the model reader, so a misreading of the model would turn both wrong and leave every generated test green. Vectors written by the user from the ICD give a second source: the generated test compares with the vector's own values, and the codec only confirms the vector when the project is validated (SR-22), which finds a wrong vector or a wrong model early without moving the oracle. A vector must name requirements; a requirement verified by test needs one (strict rule DS-4), so verification is claimed only where an independent expectation exists. Vectors stay apart from the golden files, which are a regression baseline produced by the codec. The format minor moved to 2 because an older tool must reject a file with vectors by version and not by an unknown-key error. | | D53 | Results and runtime coverage | The test results, the coverage and the toolchain of a run are files the generated CMake project writes (results/), and the lifecycle documents read them with a strict reader: a missing or damaged file is an error, so a report cannot be silently empty. The user's build measures the runtime too (opt-in, statements of the code that reaches the binary), which updates D31: the runtime headers were covered only by the repository's own tests before. The generated-header gate (100 % branch and function) is unchanged. A gap is closed by a test or justified in deviations.yaml, matched by file and function and optionally by lines so that a moved line asks for a new review; one record format serves coverage now and rule findings later. Stack values come from -fstack-usage of the -O0 coverage build and are labeled indicative. Without results strict mode checks the model only and says so. | | D54 | Runtime dossier | The runtime is hand-written, so its requirements are written and reviewed by people and not derived: they live in runtime/requirements.yaml (MIT with the library), are checked against the headers, and every unit test records the ones it verifies. The first draft came from the headers and the tests, which makes it circular; the file says so and the pull request that changes it records the reviewer. Generated low-level requirements point to the runtime requirements that realize their kind, and a requirement that only the runtime tests verify needs one, so "the runtime verifies it" is no longer a claim without evidence. Concurrency claims are analysis and the evidence is for single-threaded use with the null lock. The dossier is ours: CI produces it per release and projects refer to it. Runtime statement coverage is measured and the gaps are listed; they are closed with tests or justified in runtime/deviations.yaml. The license of the library (D43) covers the requirements file. | | D55 | Process integration | WireForge fits into the customer's DO-178C process by files and stable ids, not by a connection to their tool. The high-level requirements stay in the customer's tool; WireForge keeps a read-only snapshot of one baseline, with the tool, the baseline and a content hash, and refuses to overwrite a snapshot edited by hand. Low-level requirements are numbered in an append-only lock file, so a number is never changed or reused, also across renames. ReqIF is read and written without a dependency, with deterministic identifiers and the time of the last commit; the written files have not been validated against the schema of the standard or imported by a commercial tool yet, which the integration pages say. The tag convention and the CSV columns are interfaces: changing them is breaking. Permalinks are made only for model files and only from a committed working copy, because generated files may not be in git. The generator stays unqualified and the documents make no claim of certification. | | D56 | Change impact | docs --since REV compares the working copy with a git revision that is read with git archive into a temporary directory, so the working tree is never touched. It reports what the change did to the requirements, the low-level requirements, the generated files and declarations, the tests and the wire compatibility, and ends with the tests to run and review again. The list errs on the side of more tests: a limit can change a test that does not verify its own requirement. | | D57 | Rule checker results | WireForge does not check coding rules; it reads what the customer's licensed checker reported (SARIF 2.1.0 or cppcheck XML version 2) and puts it into code_standard.md. Only findings in generated code and the runtime count, the rest is counted. A finding is justified by a kind: rule deviation matched by tool, rule, file and function, and an unjustified finding is DS-9 under --strict. Without results the document says so and makes no conformance claim. The readers have not been tried against a licensed checker yet. | | D58 | Runtime coverage gate | The runtime line coverage gate counts every template instance that reaches a binary, as gcovr reports it, and is raised by running more code, never by excluding any. Targets that were only compiled run in the normal test run: the differential harness of every example and profile, and the fuzz target of every generated project with deterministic inputs (random bytes, every length, every read length of a link, the golden inputs cut at every length and changed at every byte). The gate follows the measurement, rounded down, and is measured with the compilers of the CI image. | | D59 | Architecture matrix | The runtime and the generated code are tested on the four combinations of 32/64 bit and little/big endian, with one x86 and one ARM target among the little-endian ones: s390x (64-bit BE), powerpc (32-bit BE), i686 and armhf (32-bit LE), aarch64 (64-bit LE) and the host. Each target is a CI job of its own that runs every suite under qemu user emulation; one required check, portability, depends on all of them. Emulation is not hardware, which the documents say. The runtime uses only atomics of pointer size, so a 32-bit target without 64-bit atomics links without libatomic; the tests follow the same rule. ARM big endian is not tested because the distributions have no toolchain for it. | | D60 | Operating-system matrix | The runtime and the generated code contain nothing that belongs to an operating system: an allow list of standard headers and no test for an OS macro, checked by a script. They are proved on Linux, Windows (three toolchains), macOS, Android and FreeRTOS. Android is built and linked for three ABIs but not run, because a Bionic binary needs the Android loader and a statically linked one aborts under user emulation; no emulator image is started in CI. FreeRTOS runs on QEMU with its own small test harness, because GoogleTest needs an operating system: it runs the generated self-tests and the runtime with the kernel's mutex as the lock. The kernel's lock is not part of the library; a lock policy is a user type, and the harness shows one. The single required check of the matrix is os-matrix. | | D61 | Coverage of generated code over any model | A 100 % coverage gate measured on four examples says little about a user's model. The claim rests on three checks: a matrix of schema features that every built and measured model set has to cover (and that the schema's properties are mapped to), valid random models generated from a fixed seed through the whole chain with the same gates, and a rule that an enum field without a default needs a member 0. The random run found defects of the generator in its first run (a test for only the first message of an interface, the interface byte order in raw decode errors, messages outside any interface, conditional messages in profiles without them), so it stays in CI and runs wider each night. Unreachable code is not excluded: it is not generated. It is evidence over many models, not a proof, and the user's gate remains. | | D62 | Project templates | A new user starts from a working project instead of a blank file: wireforge init (also an MCP argument and a field of the project creation of the REST API and the web UI) copies one of three small templates, telemetry, command and raw, and replaces its name, namespace and version. The templates are ordinary projects kept as data files; CI builds and measures them like the examples, so a template never drifts from the generator. They show the common shapes and no advanced feature (profiles, conditions, user types, requirements), which stay in the YAML. init never overwrites: the directory must be empty. | | D63 | CI check | The check a CI system runs is one command, wireforge ci, and the GitHub action and the GitLab example only call it, so every system and a developer's machine give the same answer. It validates, compares the project with the project at a git revision (the base of a pull request) for wire compatibility and the version bump, optionally builds and runs the tests, and writes one Markdown summary; the exit code is red when any of them fails. The action installs the WireForge it is part of, so pinning the action pins the tool. A base that cannot be read is reported in the summary and does not fail the check. | | D64 | Distribution | The wheel and the source distribution are built with a fixed timestamp (the last commit) and must come out the same twice (the wheel byte for byte, the source distribution file for file), carry everything the tool needs at run time, and install and work in a clean environment. Python 3.10 to 3.13 are tested; ruff and mypy are pinned to one minor version. The version has one source. A release is a tag: the workflow builds, writes an SBOM and a dependency audit that must be clean, and publishes a GitHub release; PyPI upload is a separate job behind the pypi environment (the owner approves) and the variable PUBLISH_TO_PYPI, off until a trusted publisher is configured on PyPI. The package declares both licenses as an SPDX expression (BUSL-1.1 AND MIT). | | D65 | Published protocols as examples | A model that is only checked against itself can share a wrong reading with the reference codec and the generated code. Two published protocols (Modbus RTU and Modbus TCP) are written from their specifications; their vectors are bytes from the examples of the specifications, never produced by WireForge, and an independent implementation (pymodbus, pinned) must agree byte for byte. What the schema cannot say is recorded as a finding and not bent to fit. The first comparison found a defect: a receiver on a link without a frame decoder did not check the checksum, and no receiver checked a header constant that is not the sync word; the generated receiver now does, with a test for the frame of every message. | | D66 | Coverage points | The tests of a generated project are checked against the model while they are written: the model decides which points they must exercise, each test records what it covers, and a gap stops the generation as a defect of the generator. The points are the ones where a generator went wrong before (a test for the first message only, a check that is emitted for every message but tested for one). The required set comes from the cases of the model and from predicates the code generator shares with the test writer, not from the loops that write the tests, so a skipped message shows. It does not model individual compiler branches; the random models and the coverage gate stay the evidence for those. | | D67 | Physical values and CAN databases | A field can carry scale and offset (physical = raw * scale + offset): the wire, the ranges, the defaults and the constants stay raw, the generated code adds a getter and a rounding, range-checking setter per field, and the reference codec adds the physical values to its result. The CAN database importer is written in the tool (a DBC file is a small, line-oriented format; a dependency would only be needed for the independent comparison, which cantools does in the tests, byte for byte on the example and on edge cases of both byte orders). A message takes one byte order; multiplexing, frames longer than 8 bytes and overlapping signals are refused with their line, because WireForge lays fields out one after the other and a layout that depends on a field value or on a second byte order would need a different model, and a wrong guess is worse than a refusal. --skip-unsupported lists what was left out. The CAN identifier is carried by the header of the interface (bit 31 is the extended-frame flag, as in DBC and SocketCAN), so a DBC network is an ordinary interface with the usual dispatch, framing and tests. | | D68 | Published protocol library | The models of published protocols live in protocols/ (Modbus RTU and TCP moved there from examples/; examples/ keeps the tutorials), ship in the wheel and start a project with wireforge init --protocol (also the MCP and REST creation calls and the web UI list; the template mechanism of D62 serves both). A model enters the library only with an independent implementation of the same protocol to compare against byte for byte (D65), vectors that are the examples of the documents where there are any, a README that names the source, what is covered and what is not, and the same gates as every model (100 % coverage, feature matrix, matrices, fuzz). The models are written from the public documents without copying their text, and name the owner of the protocol as not affiliated. A protocol the schema cannot say is not bent into it: a small schema decision comes first or the protocol stays out and the README says so (UBX needed none: the id is little endian class | id << 8, and a checksum that skips the sync characters is a custom checksum). | | D69 | C runtime | The generator will write C99 as well as C++17, and C code needs a runtime of its own: runtime/include/wireforge/c/, header-only and static inline, with the semantics of the C++ runtime (the status values and their order, the first error kept by the encoder and the decoder, the byte and bit rules, the checks, the CRC engine) so that the same model gives the same bytes and the same statuses in both languages. It is plain C99 and is tested as plain C (a program without a framework) with a stricter warning set than the C++ code gets, because C converts silently where C++ would need a cast. A checksum is a function over the covered bytes, not a type with a state: the encoder and the decoder have those bytes in memory, and the Python reference implementations of the custom checksums are one-shot functions as well. | | D70 | C99 code of the model | --language c writes model.h and model.c with the rules of the C++ code and the runtime of D69. The types are plain structs: an array of variable size has a count member, an enum is an integer type with a macro per member, every name starts with the namespace of the project. Checks are chained with wf_first_error so that the generated functions have no branch of their own for them, which keeps the 100 % branch gate reachable. The tests are C++ (GoogleTest) that call the C functions, and every expectation still comes from the reference codec; the test project builds the C code with the warning set of C code as errors. Functions are generated only for the types and enums that a message or an interface uses, because a function nothing calls cannot be tested and the gate is 100 %. A custom checksum is a C function over the covered bytes, named in the model (c_impl, c_include), as the Python plugins already are. User types and the interface layer are not generated in C yet. | | D71 | C99 interfaces | The interface layer of generated C is a handler struct of callbacks, one dispatch function and a link that owns its buffers, over a runtime of a ring, a frame decoder and a link (D69) that keep the behaviour of the C++ ones (the same framing rules, the same statuses, the same resynchronisation) and drop what C99 cannot express: locks and atomics. A link belongs to one thread at a time and the application guards it where it shares a ring with an interrupt. A null callback means the default (decode and forward, or ignore), so a handler can be as small as the application needs, and the generated tests cover both. Interface code is tested like the model: the cases come from the reference codec, short_frame, unknown_id and ignored are coverage points, and the 100 % gate covers the interface sources as well. | | D72 | GitHub Marketplace listing | The WireForge check action is listed from the main repository: no separate repository and no PyPI pin, because the action installs the WireForge of the ref written after uses: and stars and traffic stay with the project. Documentation names a full release tag (@v0.1.0), and no moving major tag is kept before 1.0. The licenses already in the repository serve as the end-user terms (LICENSE, runtime/LICENSE), the action collects no data, support is the issue tracker, and the listing is free. Running wireforge ci (validation, comparison with earlier revisions, generated tests) is non-production use even in commercial product repositories; this is written into the Additional Use Grant rather than only into the documentation. | | D73 | Wiki as the entry layer | The repository wiki is a short entry layer for new users: what the tool does, install, the published protocols, importers, integrations and a FAQ with the license summary. It links to docs/ instead of copying it, so there is one source of truth for the reference, and its links name a release tag so that it stays consistent with a published version. It is edited by hand by collaborators only, with no synchronisation from docs/. The licensing summary is stated as a summary that points to LICENSE, with one contact address for commercial licensing. | | D74 | Payloads without trailing zeros | An interface can send every payload without its trailing zero bytes (trim_trailing_zeros), the rule that MAVLink 2 depends on.
