It is a property of the frame, not of the message: serialize() still writes the whole payload, the frame writer shortens it with a runtime helper and the default raw handler extends a shorter payload with zeros before decoding, so the generated code gains no branch and the 100 % branch gate holds. The receiver restores zeros up to the size of the message, so every message of such an interface has a fixed size (SR-25), and switching the setting is a breaking change. A payload longer than the message stays TrailingBytes unless allow_trailing_bytes is set; the MAVLink 2 model leaves it off, because with it nothing could make its messages fail to decode and the error path of the generated handler would be unreachable. The tests the generator writes take truncated payloads out of the decode-error cases of such an interface and check the trimmed frame size of every message (FRAME_TRIM). | | D75 | Whole-byte header bit-fields | A header field may be a bit-field when it is unsigned, not a constant, a whole number of bytes wide and the header bit order follows its byte order (little with lsb_first, big with msb_first). Under those orders every such field of a bit group has bytes of its own, so generated code writes and reads it as a field of that width (write_width, wf_enc_unsigned) instead of packing bits, and the frame decoder finds a message id of any width from 1 to 8 bytes. This gives the 24-bit message id of MAVLink 2 without a new integer type. Other header bit-fields stay outside the supported subset of the interface generator. | | D76 | One tutorial that runs in CI | The tutorial (docs/tutorial/) follows one example from start to end, the MAVLink 2 link of a small drone, because a protocol readers know and an independent implementation to talk to (pymavlink) make every step checkable: the reader adds a message, generates code, builds a vehicle and sees a ground station written without WireForge understand it. The commands of the chapters run in the quickstart job with the wheel a user installs (quality/run_tutorial.py): a fenced block after <!-- tutorial: run --> runs as shown, a <!-- tutorial: hidden --> comment holds the terminal equivalent of a step done in an editor or the web UI, and blocks that need a GUI, Wireshark or an agent are not run. The example application lives next to the tutorial (examples/tutorial/drone_app/) and builds against the reader's own model. Screenshots are taken from the real web UI over a fresh workspace, with numbered marks the text refers to. | | D77 | MAVLink dialects as projects | wireforge import-mavlink reads a MAVLink XML dialect and its includes and writes a MAVLink 2 project with the frame of the published model, so every message of common.xml, ArduPilot's or a user's dialect becomes a model in one step. The CRC_EXTRA byte is computed from the definition with the rule of the MAVLink generators and written to the one list the C, C++ and Python checksum code reads, instead of being copied by hand. Fields keep their integer types although the XML names an enum, because a MAVLink receiver must accept values that a newer dialect added and an enum field would reject them; the enums are imported for their names and values. Only MAVLink 2 frames are written, and only the command line and the Python service offer the importer, since it reads files of the machine it runs on; a document type is refused, so the XML parser never expands entities. The test imports every dialect pymavlink ships and compares the byte and the field order of each message, and every message of common.xml byte for byte; a ten-message import under tests/models runs through all generated-code gates and must equal what the importer writes. | | D78 | The tutorial on a microcontroller | The vehicle of the tutorial is written once in C99 against the generated C code and a two-function transport, and runs unchanged on a desktop over UDP and as bare-metal firmware on a Cortex-M4 over its UART. The firmware runs in QEMU's MPS2 board (mps2-an386), so the chapter needs no hardware and runs in CI where the Arm toolchain and QEMU are installed; a chapter declares the tools it needs and is skipped elsewhere. For this, wireforge_generate() takes LANGUAGE c and gives a static C99 library without the C++ runtime, so a C-only cross build works. The MAVLink 2 Wireshark hook reads the CRC_EXTRA bytes from the project's crc_extra.h (found from its own place in the project, with its built-in table as the fallback), so the list of CRC_EXTRA bytes stays one file. Against ArduPilot, the tutorial shows a C ground station built from the import of the whole ardupilotmega.xml talking to the ArduCopter simulator; that step needs a download from ArduPilot and is not run in CI. |

docs.title: Fitting WireForge into a DO-178C process
docs.text:
WireForge's code, tests and documents fit into your DO-178C process as they are. Your high-level requirements stay in your own requirements tool. WireForge produces the low-level requirements that refine them, the code, the tests and the results in the formats your tools read (ReqIF, CSV, JUnit, Cobertura) and with your id scheme. Every baseline comes with a traceability matrix and a mapping to the DAL C objectives. Nothing is locked in: it is all plain text in git.

Generated code still goes through your verification process: WireForge automates that verification and its evidence; it does not remove it. The generator is not a qualified tool. No document says that a result is certified or compliant. The documents are evidence for, and support, the objectives of your process (docs/LIFECYCLE.md).

docs.title: Who does what
docs.text:
WireForge You (the applicant) High-level requirements imports a snapshot of a baseline; never edits them write and baseline them in your tool Low-level requirements derives them from the model, numbers them, exports them review them, bring them into your tool Code and tests generates them with the requirement ids in comments and test properties review, build and run them on the target Results and coverage reads JUnit and coverage of a run and reports gaps run the tests, justify the gaps Traceability matrix derives it; never maintained by hand scan it in your tool if you want it there DAL C objectives maps documents to objectives, marks the ones that are yours planning, quality assurance, certification liaison

Where each kind of data lives is in docs/integration/README.md. The mapping of documents to objectives is do178c_dal_c.md in the documents (docs/LIFECYCLE.md).

docs.title: A thirty minute path on example 02
docs.text:
Work on a copy of examples/02_multi_interface_avionics.

# 1. take a baseline of high-level requirements from your tool (here: a small ReqIF sample)
wireforge reqs-import avionics requirements/srs_sample.reqif --baseline SRS-B1
# 2. give the low-level requirements numbers that never change
wireforge reqs-lock avionics
# 3. generate code and tests
wireforge generate avionics -o build/gen --tests
# 4. run the tests with coverage of the generated code and of the runtime
wireforge test avionics -o build/gen --coverage-runtime --cmake-arg=-DWIREFORGE_COVERAGE_RUNTIME_MIN_LINE=0
# 5. write the documents for the baseline, with permalinks and the ReqIF export
wireforge docs avionics -o build/docs --results build/gen/avionics_demo/generated_tests/build/coverage \
  --export reqif,csv --source-url 'https://git.example.com/repo/blob/{commit}/{path}#L{line}'
Step 1 replaces the requirements section of the project with the snapshot, so remove an inline copy of the same ids first. --strict makes docs fail when a reviewer would reject the model; the rules are in docs/LIFECYCLE.md.

docs.title: What is an id
docs.text: A low-level requirement is identified by a key made of names (SensorReading.temperature.RANGE) and shown as LLR-<key>. With llr_ids.lock (created by wireforge reqs-lock) it is shown with your numbering, for example SWLLR-00017. A number is never changed or reused, also when the element is renamed (wireforge reqs-rename-key) or removed. The id is the same in code comments, test properties and every document.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The ReqIF files WireForge writes have not been checked against the XSD of the standard or imported by a commercial tool yet; the pages in docs/integration say what to try first.
  • There is no live connection to a requirements tool (no OSLC, no REST). Files are exchanged and kept in git.
  • Tests on the target hardware and the process data around them are yours.

docs.title: WireForge user guide
docs.text:
WireForge turns a description of binary messages (YAML, edited by hand, in the web UI or by an AI agent) into C++17 code that serializes, validates, frames and dispatches them without heap, exceptions or RTTI, plus a GoogleTest project that proves the code against a reference codec. The wire format is the one you describe: the generator never adds bytes.

New to WireForge? The tutorial builds a MAVLink 2 drone link step by step: the web UI, the code in an application, the tests, CI, Wireshark and AI agents.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Python 3.10 to 3.13. 

pip install "wireforge[server,mcp,import]"   # or, in a checkout: pip install -e ".[server,mcp,import]"
pip install "wireforge[oidc]"                # OIDC login for the server (docs/SERVER.md)
A C++17 compiler, CMake 3.21+ and (for the tests) Ninja or Make are needed to build generated code. Docker: docker build -t wireforge . && docker run -p 8000:8000 -v "$PWD/projects:/workspace" wireforge serves the web UI and API on port 8000 with the toolchain inside; it has no token by default, so read Deployment and operation before exposing it.

docs.title: In CI
docs.text: wireforge ci <project> --base <revision> --test validates the project, compares it with the base of a pull request (wire compatibility and the version bump each changed interface needs) and builds and runs the generated tests, with one Markdown summary. The repository has a GitHub action for it and a GitLab example (docs/integration/github_actions.md).

docs.title: Quickstart (about 5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Start from a template or a published protocol (or skip to step 1 with your own ICD): 
    wireforge init demo --template telemetry      # also: command, raw; --list shows them
wireforge init gps --protocol ubx             # a published protocol, see "Published protocols"
wireforge validate demo && wireforge test demo -o build/demo
    The template is a working project with comments; change the names, fields and limits to match your protocol. The web UI has the same start under "New project"; its "Generate" tab shows the generated code and downloads it with the test project.
  2. Describe messages. Write a project.yaml (docs/SCHEMA_SPEC.md, examples/), or import an ICD table, a C header, a CAN database (wireforge import-dbc) or a MAVLink XML dialect (wireforge import-mavlink, docs/IMPORT.md): 
    wireforge import-icd examples/icd/telemetry_icd.csv demo --name telemetry --namespace demo::imu --endian little
  3. Add an interface (header, framing, the messages it carries): 
    wireforge upsert demo interfaces imu_link '{ version: "1.0.0", direction: rx,
  header: { fields: [{ name: msgId, type: u16, role: message_id }, { name: length, type: u8, role: payload_length }] },
  framing: { kind: length_prefixed, max_frame_size: 64 }, messages: [ImuSample, Heartbeat] }'
  4. Validate and inspect: wireforge validate demo, wireforge analyze demo (sizes, offsets, bit maps, frame and buffer sizes per profile), wireforge encode demo ImuSample '{ sensorId: 3 }' --interface imu_link.
  5. Generate and test: wireforge test demo -o generated generates the code and the test project, builds it and runs every test; --coverage runs the coverage target instead.
  6. Use it in your build: 
    find_package(WireForge 0.1 REQUIRED)        # -DWireForge_DIR=$(wireforge cmake-dir), or an installed prefix
wireforge_generate(imu_model PROJECT ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/demo)
target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE imu_model)
    LANGUAGE c gives a C99 library instead (docs/CODEGEN.md). See examples/cmake_consumer/ (quality/run_quickstart.sh runs all of the above from a fresh wheel and checks that it takes less than 15 minutes).

docs.title: Working with projects
docs.text:
• Files are the source of truth (docs/CLI.md): edit YAML by hand, with wireforge set/upsert/remove, in the web UI or through MCP; wireforge fmt keeps one canonical layout so every way of editing gives minimal diffs.
  • Profiles select platform variants (defines, if: conditions); every tool works per profile.
  • Versions: interface.version follows semver; wireforge compat old/ new/ (or the UI's Versions tab) tells whether a change is breaking, compatible or documentation only.
  • Team server: wireforge serve --workspace projects/ (docs/SERVER.md, docs/UI.md).
  • AI agents: wireforge mcp --workspace projects/ (docs/MCP.md).
  • Wireshark: wireforge wireshark demo -o demo.lua writes a Lua dissector plugin for every interface (docs/WIRESHARK.md).

docs.title: Generated code
docs.text:
With --language c the code is C99 instead (model.h, model.c; docs/CODEGEN.md, runtime in runtime/include/wireforge/c/).

model.hpp (types with defaults, validate(), sizes, serialize()/deserialize()), one header per interface (ids, encode_frame(), Handler, Endpoint, Link) and user_prelude.hpp; see docs/CODEGEN.md. The runtime is header-only (runtime/include/wireforge/, docs/RUNTIME.md). Bare-metal builds define WIREFORGE_NO_STD_MUTEX.

docs.title: Quality and safety
docs.text: Zero warnings from every compiler and analyzer, a 95 % line-coverage gate on generated code (the examples reach 100 %), differential and fuzz testing against the reference codec, big-endian and 32-bit test runs, no-heap evidence and a trace report from model rows to code and tests (quality/QUALITY_POLICY.md, docs/SAFETY.md).

docs.title: Published protocols
docs.text:
wireforge init <dir> --protocol <name> (or the same choice under "New project" in the web UI) copies the model of a published protocol that is written from its public documents and checked against an independent implementation of it (byte for byte, in tests/python/). Each model has a README with its source, what it covers and what it does not.

Protocol Covers Independent check modbus_rtu Modbus RTU: read holding registers, write single register, exceptions; CRC-16/MODBUS sent low byte first; vectors from the examples of the specification pymodbus modbus_tcp Modbus TCP: the MBAP header with a length, one message per interface (vectors of the specification) crsf CRSF (radio link to flight controller): the frame and HEARTBEAT, BATTERY_SENSOR, LINK_STATISTICS, one message per interface crsf-parser j1939 SAE J1939: the identifier word (priority, PGN, source address) and the groups EEC1, CCVS, ET1 cantools mavlink1 MAVLink 1: the frame and HEARTBEAT, ATTITUDE, GLOBAL_POSITION_INT, COMMAND_LONG; a checksum that adds the CRC_EXTRA byte of the message pymavlink mavlink2 MAVLink 2 (what current autopilots speak): the frame with the 24-bit message id, payloads without their trailing zero bytes, HEARTBEAT, GPS_RAW_INT and COMMAND_ACK with extension fields, ATTITUDE, GLOBAL_POSITION_INT, COMMAND_LONG; a Lua checksum hook for Wireshark pymavlink ubx u-blox UBX: the frame, ACK-ACK, ACK-NAK, CFG-RATE, NAV-PVT, MON-VER; Fletcher-8 that skips the sync characters pyubx2

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Example Shows examples/01_basic_telemetry one interface: sync/id/length header, CRC-32 trailer, enum, nested struct, counted array examples/02_multi_interface_avionics avionics-style node: three interfaces (sync+length with CRC-16, raw, length-prefixed), platform profiles with conditional fields, lsb-first bit-fields, optional field, fill array, user-defined checksum, application constants examples/03_edge_cases corner cases: zero counts, nested optional, signed bit-fields, u64, wire constants examples/04_user_type an opaque field type backed by application code examples/07_can_dbc a CAN network imported from a DBC file: Intel and Motorola signals, factor and offset, value tables as enums, an extended identifier (wireforge import-dbc) examples/icd/ ICD sources for the importers (CSV table, C header) examples/cmake_consumer/ an application built with find_package(WireForge)

docs.title: Importers
docs.text: wireforge import-icd <source> <directory> --name <project> [--namespace NS] [--version V] [--endian big|little] [--message Struct ...] creates a new single-file project (<directory>/project.yaml, canonical layout) and validates it. The server offers the same as POST /api/import (format: csv, h, or xlsx with base64 content); Python: wireforge.service.import_icd, wireforge.importers.from_csv/from_xlsx/from_c_header.

docs.title: ICD tables (CSV, Excel)
docs.text:
One row per field; Excel reads the first sheet (pip install 'wireforge[import]' for openpyxl). Columns (header row, any order, only name, field and type are required):

Column Meaning section message (default) or type; consecutive rows of one name form one entry name message or type name id message id (first row of the message; hex like 0x0110 stays hex) field, type field name and type (builtin, enum or type name) bits bit-field width occurs empty: one value; N: fixed array; 0..N: counted array (0..1 optional field); M..N with a minimum; fill..N: fills the payload count count field or expression of a counted array min, max, default numbers or expressions units, description documentation

Sample: examples/icd/telemetry_icd.csv (a bit-field type, a nested struct, an optional field, a counted array).

docs.title: C headers
docs.text:
#define NAME <integer> becomes a define (defines without a value, such as include guards, are skipped), enum an enum (u8, u16 or u32 by the largest value, i32 with negative values), every struct (also typedef struct) whose members are uint8_t ... int64_t, bool, char, float, double, earlier structs or enums becomes a type: arrays T name[N] are fixed arrays (N may be a define), bit-fields T name : n keep their width. Structs named with --message become messages (ids 1, 2, ... in header order); without --message every struct that no other struct uses is a message. Pointers, unions, unknown types and non-integer defines are reported with file and line; nothing is written then. Sample: examples/icd/sensors.h.

The importers write the definition only; byte order, interfaces, framing and checksums are added afterwards in the editor, the CLI (wireforge set/upsert) or by hand.

docs.title: CAN databases (DBC)
docs.text:
wireforge import-dbc <file.dbc> <directory> --name <project> [--namespace NS] [--version V] [--node NODE] [--skip-unsupported] writes a complete project, including the interfaces (POST /api/import with format: dbc, node and skip_unsupported; Python: wireforge.service.import_dbc). The example is examples/07_can_dbc.

DBC WireForge BO_ message message with the CAN identifier as id; the frame is padded with reserved bits to the data length SG_ signal field with bits; the type is the smallest one that holds the signal (u8..u64, i8..i64) Intel signals (@1) little-endian, LSB-first message Motorola signals (@0) big-endian, MSB-first message; the start bit (the most significant bit, counted in the usual DBC way) becomes a position in the bit stream factor, offset scale, offset (omitted when 1 and 0) [min\|max] (physical) raw min, max, narrowed to whole raw values with a note; omitted when the signal has no limits or the limits are the range of the type VAL_ an enum <Message>_<Signal> (a member without a value 0 makes the first member the default); a table that cannot be an enum (equal member names, factor, offset, values outside the width) is kept in the description SIG_VALTYPE_ 1, 2 f32, f64 (the signal must fill 4 or 8 whole bytes) CM_ description of the message or the signal GenMsgCycleTime sentence in the description of the message GenSigStartValue default transmitter, receivers with --node N: interface N_tx (messages N sends) and N_rx (messages N receives); without: one interface can (both)

The interfaces have a header of canId (u32, the message id; bit 31 is the extended-frame flag, as in the DBC file and in SocketCAN) and dlc (u8, the payload length) and the length_prefixed framing with a frame of at most 13 bytes. The importer describes the data of a CAN frame; the transport that delivers canId and dlc is the application's.

What cannot be expressed is an error with file and line, or, with --skip-unsupported, a note and the message left out: multiplexed signals (M, mN), extended multiplexing (SG_MUL_VAL_), frames of more than 8 bytes (CAN FD), signals of both byte orders in one message, overlapping signals and signals outside the data length, a factor of 0, and floating point signals that do not fill whole bytes. Statements that do not change a frame (VERSION, BU_, the other BA_ attributes, environment variables, signal groups) are counted in the notes.

docs.title: MAVLink dialects (XML)
docs.text:
wireforge import-mavlink <dialect.xml> <directory> --name <project> [--namespace NS] [--version V] [--message NAME ...] writes a complete MAVLink 2 project from a MAVLink XML message definition file, such as common.xml, ardupilotmega.xml or your own dialect (Python: wireforge.service.import_mavlink). The files the dialect includes (<include>) are read from its directory, each once. --message (repeatable, MAVLink names such as HEARTBEAT) takes only those messages and the enums they use.

XML WireForge <message> message HEARTBEAT → Heartbeat with the message id; fields time_boot_ms → timeBootMs (a C++ keyword gets the suffix Value, with a note) field order the order MAVLink sends: the base fields by the size of their type, largest first (equal sizes keep their order), then the <extensions/> fields as written uint8_t .. int64_t, float, double u8 .. i64, f32, f64 char[N], T[N] char with occurs: {max: N} (zero padded, as MAVLink strings), a fixed array uint8_t_mavlink_version u8 with const: 3 units, description units, description; an enum attribute and extension fields are named in the description <enum> an enum of the project with the smallest unsigned type of its values; an entry without a value takes the next one, 2**N values are read; an entry with the value of an earlier one is left out with a note

The interface link is the one of the published MAVLink 2 model (wireforge init --protocol mavlink2): the 24-bit message id, payloads without their trailing zero bytes (trim_trailing_zeros) and the checksum with the CRC_EXTRA byte of each message. The importer computes that byte from the definition, as the MAVLink generators do (the name of the message and the type, name and array length of its base fields), and writes the list to app/include/mav2sum/crc_extra.h, which the Wireshark hook wireshark/mav2sum.lua reads too (with a copy of the list as its fallback); the checksum code itself is copied from the published model. Fields keep their integer types even when they name an enum, because a MAVLink receiver must accept values a newer dialect added. Signed frames are refused, as in the published model.

tests/python/test_mavlink_xml.py imports every dialect pymavlink ships and compares the CRC_EXTRA byte and the field order of every message with pymavlink, and encodes every message of common.xml to the bytes pymavlink packs. tests/models/mavlink_import (ten messages of common.xml) runs through all generated-code gates.

The file is read without a document type: a dialect with <!DOCTYPE or <!ENTITY is refused. The importer is a command-line and Python function only; the server and the MCP server do not offer it.

docs.title: Layout analyzer and ICD export
docs.text:
python -m wireforge.layout <project> [--profile P] [--format markdown|csv|json] [-o FILE] validates the project and reports, per profile (or once without profiles):

  • Messages: minimum and maximum encoded size, and one row per field: byte offset (a range after variable-size fields), size range, bit positions inside the bit-group container (bit 0 = least significant bit, following the message's bit_order), occurrence (3, 0..5, count trackCount, fill, 0..16), range, default/const, role (const, reserved, checksum <name>, header roles), if: condition, units and description. Fields of nested structs are flattened (accel.x); fields of array elements are shown for the first element (tracks[].id).
  • Interfaces: header and trailer field tables, effective message ids (per-interface overrides applied), payload and frame size ranges, the largest payload, the frame buffer size (frame_size/max_frame_size or header + largest payload + trailer) and the RAM of the generated link: receive ring (buffers.rx_bytes, default twice the frame buffer) + receive frame + transmit frame buffer. The per-profile total is the sum over all interfaces.

Excluded from the RAM budget: the decoded message object on the receiving stack (its size depends on the compiler), decoder/dispatcher bookkeeping (a few words) and the transport's own buffers.

Exports: Markdown is an ICD document (one section per profile, interface and message), CSV has one row per field of every message, header and trailer (profile, owner, path, type, offset_min, offset_max, size_min, size_max, bit_high, bit_low, group_size, occurs, range, default, role, condition, units, description), JSON is the full report (wireforge.layout.analyze(project).to_dict()).

The numbers equal the generated code: the generated test project checks min_wire_size(), max_wire_size(), kHeaderSize, kTrailerSize, max_payload_size(), kMaxFrameSize, kRxBufferBytes and kTxBufferBytes of every message and interface against the analyzer with static_asserts, for every profile.

docs.title: Requirements, design and test documents
docs.text: wireforge docs <project> -o <dir> writes the documents a software lifecycle needs from the model: requirements, design, test specification, traceability and the checklists around them. The same text comes from GET /api/projects/{id}/docs (a zip) and the MCP tool lifecycle_docs. The output depends only on the model: no date, user name or absolute path is written, so the same model gives the same bytes and the files diff cleanly.

docs.title: What is written
docs.text:
File Content index.md baseline (model hash, tool version), list of documents, counts, result of the strict rules, limits requirements.md, .csv high-level requirements, low-level requirements derived from the model, derived requirements design.md architecture overview, generated files, interfaces (header, trailer, messages, buffers per profile), messages and types, status codes and the requirements behind them, resources interfaces_coupling.md data coupling table per interface, control coupling, assumptions test_spec.md, .csv every generated test: executable, profile, kind, oracle, requirements verified, procedure, expected result test_report.md test counts; results are not part of this run ("Test results: not provided.") traceability.md, .csv requirement to model element to LLR to code to test, and tests back to requirements, with the gaps environment.md model files with sha256, WireForge, Python and library versions code_standard.md rules the generated code follows and the evidence for each review_checklists.md checklists for requirements, design, code and tests; items WireForge can decide are answered ([auto: PASS]), the rest are open boxes for the reviewer do178c_dal_c.md which document is evidence for which DO-178C objective at DAL C; objectives the applicant owns are marked

The directory is created when missing. Only files with these names are written; nothing else in it is touched.

docs.title: Who writes what
docs.text: The high-level requirements are yours: write them in the requirements section and point model elements at them with reqs (docs/SCHEMA_SPEC.md section 17). WireForge derives the low-level requirements, links them to the generated tests and writes everything down. A low-level requirement without a high-level one is derived; derived requirements are listed so they can go to the system safety assessment. They are not an error.

docs.title: --strict
docs.text:
Without --strict the command only fails when the project is invalid. With it, the exit code is 1 when a reviewer would reject the model; each finding is printed and listed in index.md:

Rule Finding DS-1 the project defines no requirements DS-2 a message or interface without any high-level requirement behind it DS-3 a low-level requirement without a generated test (requirements the runtime tests verify are exempt) DS-4 a requirement verified by test that no model element uses, or that has no requirement vector

With no requirements only DS-1 is reported. The documents are written in any case.

docs.title: Stable ids, import and export
docs.text:
wireforge reqs-lock writes llr_ids.lock, which gives every low-level requirement a number (SWLLR-00017, or the format you choose) that never changes, is never given again and follows an element through a rename (reqs-rename-key). With the lock file the numbers show in the code comments, the test properties and every document; without it the ids are LLR-<key>. Strict rule DS-8 reports a requirement that has no number yet.

wireforge reqs-import takes a baseline of the high-level requirements of your tool (ReqIF or CSV) as a read-only snapshot, requirements/hlr_snapshot.yaml, with the tool, the baseline name and the hash of the file; a snapshot edited by hand is refused. docs --export reqif writes llr.reqifz, the low-level requirements for your tool, and --source-url 'https://.../{commit}/{path}#L{line}' turns model locations into permalinks (the working copy must be committed). index.md names the baseline: commit, snapshot, number lock, tool and runtime versions. The page docs/DO178C.md shows the whole path; docs/integration lists what to set up per tool.

docs.title: Test results and coverage
docs.text:
wireforge docs <project> -o <dir> --results <build> adds what a test run produced (docs/CODEGEN.md, "Results of a test run"): test_report.md gets the results per executable and per requirement, the failures, the coverage of the generated code and of the runtime, and the uncovered lines with or without a justification from deviations.yaml; resources.md gets the stack use; environment.md the toolchain; traceability.csv a result column. The run comes from wireforge test <project> -o <dir> --coverage-runtime, which prints the build directory. A missing or damaged result file is an error, never an empty report. The server does not build, so its /docs route has no results.

Strict mode adds three rules when results are given: DS-5 a failed or skipped test, DS-6 generated code below 100 % statement coverage or runtime coverage that was not measured, DS-7 an uncovered line without a justification. Without --results, --strict checks the model only and index.md says "Results: not provided". The generated tests alone do not execute every statement of the runtime, so DS-7 lists what remains; close it with tests or justify it.

docs.title: The runtime
docs.text: The generated code relies on the runtime library, which is hand-written. Its requirements are in runtime/requirements.yaml; the project documents show, for each low-level requirement, the runtime requirements that realize its kind (Runtime column of requirements.md) and the runtime version. A requirement that only the runtime tests verify (an unknown message id) counts as tested only when a runtime requirement realizes it, otherwise strict rule DS-3 reports it. The dossier of the runtime itself is ours: wireforge docs --runtime produces it in CI for every release (docs/RUNTIME.md, "Requirements"), and a project refers to it instead of producing it again.

docs.title: Two kinds of expectation
docs.text: Most generated tests take their expected result from the reference codec of WireForge (oracle reference-codec). A mistake in how the model is read would then be in both the codec and the generated code, and the tests would stay green. Requirement vectors (docs/SCHEMA_SPEC.md section 18) are written by you from the ICD; their tests carry the oracle hlr-vector in test_spec.md. A requirement verified by test needs at least one vector (rule DS-4); one verified by analysis or review does not, and is listed instead.

docs.title: What this is not
docs.text:
These documents are evidence for your own process. WireForge does not claim that any output is certified or compliant, and the code generator is not qualified: the generated code is verified like hand-written code, and the documents show that verification (requirement, test, result). The correctness of the high-level requirements, tests on the target and the process around them (planning, configuration management, quality assurance, certification liaison) remain yours. The objective table in do178c_dal_c.md uses our own wording and the objective numbers; confirm the rows marked check against your licensed copy of DO-178C.

quality/run_evidence.sh writes the documents of every example to build/evidence/docs_<project>/.

docs.title: Change impact
docs.text: wireforge docs <project> -o <dir> --since <git-revision> also writes impact.md and impact.csv: what a change did since that revision. It lists the high-level requirements that were added, removed or reworded (and a changed baseline of the requirement snapshot), the low-level requirements that were added, removed, reworded or got other parents, the generated files and the declarations in them that changed, the generated tests that were added, removed or changed, and the wire compatibility result of the interfaces. The last section is the list of tests to run and review again: every test that verifies a changed requirement and every test that changed. A test that uses a value derived from a limit changes when the limit changes, so a limit can reach more tests than its own requirement. The old baseline is read from git (git archive) into a temporary directory; the working copy is the new one.

docs.title: Coding standard and rule checkers
docs.text:
WireForge does not check coding rules. docs/CODING_RULES.md maps the categories of MISRA C++ and AUTOSAR C++14 to the checks that run on generated code and the runtime. A conformance claim needs the results of a licensed checker: wireforge docs <project> -o <dir> --rule-findings report.sarif (repeatable) reads SARIF 2.1.0 or cppcheck XML version 2 and adds the section "Rule findings" to code_standard.md. Only findings in generated headers and in the runtime headers count; the number of findings elsewhere is stated. Per tool and rule, the section lists the findings that have no deviation and the deviations nobody used.

A finding is justified in deviations.yaml with kind: rule: the tool name (case does not matter), the rule as the tool writes it, a file glob, optionally a function glob, the category (justified, false-positive or not-applicable), the rationale and the reviewer. --strict reports DS-9 for every group of findings without a deviation. Without --rule-findings the section says that no results were provided and DS-9 is not evaluated. The MCP tool lifecycle_docs takes rule_findings, a list of files inside the workspace. How to export a report from common tools is in docs/integration/rule_checkers.md.

docs.title: MCP server
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[mcp]", then wireforge mcp --workspace <dir> serves the Model Context Protocol on stdio (official Python SDK, MCPServer). Every subdirectory of the workspace with a project.yaml is a project. Generated code goes to <workspace>/.wireforge/generated/. Code: wireforge.mcp_server.

Example client configuration: 

{ "mcpServers": { "wireforge": { "command": "wireforge", "args": ["mcp", "--workspace", "/path/to/projects"] } } }

Tool What it does CLI equivalent list_projects projects of the workspace ls create_project(project, name, namespace?, version?, template?) new project, empty or from a template (telemetry, command, raw) wireforge init list_messages(project) messages (with ids), types, interfaces wireforge analyze get_message(project, name) definition of a message or type as written wireforge get upsert_struct(project, section, name, definition, dry_run?) create/update a type or message wireforge upsert upsert_entry(project, section, name, definition, dry_run?) create/update a checksum, enum, interface, profile, define wireforge set validate_project(project) issues with file, line and JSON pointer wireforge validate generate_code(project, tests?) C++ code and the GoogleTest project; lists the files wireforge generate --tests run_tests(project, coverage?, coverage_runtime?) build and run the generated tests (or the coverage target) wireforge test analyze_layout(project, profile?, export?) sizes, offsets, bit maps, frames, link RAM wireforge analyze requirements_import(project, path, baseline, tool?) take a baseline of high-level requirements from a file inside the workspace wireforge reqs-import requirements_lock(project) number the low-level requirements in llr_ids.lock wireforge reqs-lock lifecycle_docs(project, strict, results_dir?, rule_findings?) requirements, design, test and traceability documents in <workspace>/.wireforge/docs/<project>/ wireforge docs wireshark_dissector(project) Wireshark Lua plugin in <workspace>/.wireforge/generated/wireshark/<project>.lua wireforge wireshark compat_check(project, old_project? \| revision?) compatibility with another project or a git revision wireforge compat encode_sample(project, message, value?, interface?, profile?) payload/frame hex; without value a sample with every field set wireforge encode decode_hex(project, hex_bytes, message? \| interface, profile?) decoded payload or frame wireforge decode

Every result has ok, issues, data and text; writes with dry_run: true return the unified diff and change nothing. Bad arguments (unknown project, section or message, malformed hex) are tool errors. Custom checksum plugins (plugins/*.py) are executed, so serve trusted workspaces only.

docs.title: Agent scenario
docs.text:
quality/agent_scenario.py plays an agent that reads a short ICD text (a deterministic parser stands in for the language model), creates the project, checksum, messages and interface through the tools, validates, generates and runs the generated tests with a real build (quality/run_generated_tests.sh); tests/python/test_mcp.py runs the same scenario with the build replaced and covers every tool and error path.

results_dir is the build_dir returned by run_tests; a directory outside the workspace output is refused.

docs.title: C++ runtime (runtime/include/wireforge/)
docs.text:
Header-only C++17. No heap, no exceptions, no RTTI, no OS headers, no host-endianness or struct-layout assumptions. Every fallible call returns wireforge::Status.

Header Content status.hpp Status, is_ok(), to_string() (see Status codes below) config.hpp build options: WIREFORGE_CONFIG_HEADER, WIREFORGE_NO_STD_MUTEX, WIREFORGE_DEFAULT_LOCK, WIREFORGE_CRC_TABLELESS version.hpp runtime version constants span.hpp Span<T> (dynamic extent, explicit constructors, subspan/first), make_span array_access.hpp array_at(): std::array element access without the exception path of at() static_vector.hpp StaticVector<T, N> (occurs storage: count + std::array), FixedString<N> (char arrays, always zero-terminated) lock.hpp lock policy contract is_lock_policy_v, NullLock, StdMutexLock, DefaultLock, ScopedLock, RelaxedCounter bit_utils.hpp BitOrder, masks, two's complement helpers, reflect, narrow_to, BitPacker / BitUnpacker byte_io.hpp Endian, store_unsigned/load_unsigned, ByteWriter, ByteReader (ints 1..8 bytes, f32/f64, bytes, bit groups, patching) ring_buffer.hpp SpscByteRing (lock-free), StaticSpscByteRing<N>, LockedByteRing<L> frame_layout.hpp FieldLocation shared by decoder and dispatcher payload_trim.hpp trimmed_size, ZeroExtended<N>: payloads sent without their trailing zero bytes frame_decoder.hpp FrameFormat, FrameDecoder<Checksum> (fixed, sync+length, length-prefixed; checksum verify; resync; counters) delegate.hpp Delegate<R(Args...)>: non-owning free/member/callable reference, no heap dispatcher.hpp RawMessage (payload and frame), Dispatcher<N, L> (header ids, fallback, frozen table), RawDispatcher<L> transport.hpp transport requirements is_transport_v, ITransport base, LoopbackTransport<N> link.hpp Link<Transport, Decoder, Dispatch, MaxFrame, RxCapacity, L>, Unframed, PollResult checksum.hpp checksum contract is_checksum_v, compute_checksum, Crc<...> (Rocksoft), Crc32, Crc16CcittFalse codec_support.hpp Encoding, Encoder/Decoder with a sticky first error (used by generated codecs) validation.hpp range, bit-width and count checks used by generated validate(); status_if(), size_if_ok() and first_error() keep generated code free of branches expr_support.hpp integer helpers used by generated size and count expressions

docs.title: Status codes
docs.text:
enum class Status : std::uint8_t; every fallible call returns one, nothing throws.

Code Meaning Ok Success BufferTooSmall The output buffer cannot hold the encoded data Truncated The input ended before the data was complete OutOfRange A value violates its min/max, enum or bit-width range CountExceedsMax An element count is above the capacity (or below the minimum) ConstMismatch A constant field differs from its declared value ChecksumMismatch A received checksum does not match the recomputed one UnknownMessageId A message id is not known on this interface InvalidLength A length field is inconsistent with the frame or buffer TrailingBytes The payload was not fully consumed InvalidState The API was misused (invalid argument or call sequence)

docs.title: Byte and bit IO
docs.text:
• Integers are written byte by byte with shifts; widths 1..8 bytes; signed values as two's complement, decoded with explicit sign extension (no implementation-defined conversions). Floats go through their IEEE-754 bit pattern (D11).
  • A failing call changes neither the position nor the output. write_unsigned_at patches an already written range (length fields, checksums); peek_unsigned_at inspects a header without consuming it.
  • Bit groups (D19): BitPacker(total_bits, order) collects fields into one container integer, write_bits writes it with the message endianness; read_bits + BitUnpacker reverse it. Endianness is a function argument, so a constant argument in generated code is resolved at compile time (all IO except floats is constexpr).
  • Encoder::write_bytes(Span<const std::uint8_t>) / Decoder::read_bytes(Span<std::uint8_t>) copy bytes onto/from the wire unchanged, no endian or bit-order transform: the only IO a user type's own encode/decode needs.
  • Encoder::write_width(value, width) / Decoder::read_width(value, width) write and read an unsigned value in a number of bytes smaller than its type (a 24-bit header field); a value that does not fit is OutOfRange.
  • payload_trim.hpp: trimmed_size(payload) is the size of a payload without its trailing zero bytes (the first byte stays) and ZeroExtended<N> gives a shorter payload back as N bytes padded with zeros, for interfaces with trim_trailing_zeros. The C runtime has wf_trimmed_size() and wf_zero_extend() (wireforge/c/trim.h).

docs.title: C runtime
docs.text: runtime/include/wireforge/c/ is the runtime for C99 code (#include <wireforge/c/wireforge.h>, or the single headers): header-only, static inline, no heap, no global state, no operating system. Its names are the ones of the C++ runtime with a wf_ prefix, and the rules are the same: wf_status has the values and the order of wireforge::Status (WF_OK, WF_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL, ...); wf_writer/wf_reader and wf_bit_packer/wf_bit_unpacker do the byte and bit IO of byte_io.hpp and bit_utils.hpp; wf_encoder/wf_decoder keep the first error like Encoder/Decoder; wf_check_* are the checks of validation.hpp, with the value passed as int64_t, uint64_t or double; wf_crc() is the parametric CRC (bitwise, without a table); wf_expr_* are the helpers of generated expressions. A checksum of a field is a function uint64_t f(const uint8_t *data, size_t length) over the covered bytes. For interfaces there is wf_ring (a byte ring over caller storage), wf_frame_decoder (sync and length, length prefixed and fixed framing, a checksum, resynchronisation, counters: frame_decoder.hpp) and wf_link (reads a wf_transport into the ring, dispatches every frame, sends frames, counts bytes and frames: link.hpp). They have no locks and no atomics (C99 has none): a link belongs to one thread at a time, and an interrupt handler that fills a ring guards it with a critical section of the application. The C runtime is tested by tests/c/runtime_test.c and tests/c/link_test.c (plain C99, no framework) and is compiled with the warning set of C code (-Wall -Wextra -Wconversion -Wsign-conversion -Wshadow ... as errors; /W4 /WX for MSVC).

docs.title: Thread safety
docs.text:
• SpscByteRing: exactly one producer (write) and one consumer (peek, read, consume); indices run in [0, 2*capacity) so the whole storage is usable; release/acquire atomics publish data. reset() needs both sides idle.
  • LockedByteRing<L> runs every operation under lock policy L; write_all keeps records from concurrent producers whole.
  • Lock policies are template parameters. An RTOS port provides a default-constructible type with lock() noexcept and unlock() noexcept and sets WIREFORGE_DEFAULT_LOCK (and WIREFORGE_NO_STD_MUTEX to drop <mutex>), D17.

docs.title: Checksums (D4, D16)
docs.text: Crc<Width, Poly, Init, RefIn, RefOut, XorOut, UseTable> covers widths 1..64 with a left-aligned 64-bit register; the table mode shares one 2 KiB constexpr table per polynomial, the table-less mode loops over bits. Custom algorithms follow the contract in checksum.hpp; generated code asserts is_checksum_v<Impl>.

docs.title: Frame decoding
docs.text: FrameDecoder<Checksum> reads from any ring with size/capacity/peek/consume. Incomplete frames stay in the ring, so results do not depend on chunking. next() returns Ok (frame copied out), Truncated (need more bytes) or a rejection (InvalidLength, ChecksumMismatch, BufferTooSmall) after which decoding continues. With resync a rejection skips one byte and rescans; without it every buffered byte is dropped. Bytes that cannot start a frame (wrong sync) are skipped silently and counted in discarded_bytes. Framing none needs no decoder (each transport read is one frame).

docs.title: Dispatching
docs.text: Handlers are registered (add, set_fallback, set_handler) before start(), under the lock policy. start() sorts and freezes the table; afterwards dispatch()/dispatch_frame() take no lock and can run on several threads, and registration returns InvalidState. Unknown ids go to the fallback handler or return UnknownMessageId. Handlers receive a RawMessage with the payload and the whole frame. dispatch(id, payload) passes the payload as both spans; dispatch_frame() slices the payload out of the frame. Both spans are valid only during the call.

docs.title: Transport and link
docs.text: A transport has send(Span<const uint8_t>) -> size_t and receive(Span<uint8_t>) -> size_t, both non-blocking. An existing driver interface is connected by a small adapter class, either a plain type or derived from ITransport. Link::poll() (one receiving thread) moves transport bytes into its ring, decodes and dispatches every complete frame and returns counts plus the last error. Link::send(encode) runs the encoder on the preallocated tx buffer under the tx lock and hands the frame to the transport; a transport that stops accepting bytes mid-frame gives BufferTooSmall (the receiver resynchronises). With Unframed each transport read is one frame; a read longer than MaxFrame is rejected as InvalidLength and whatever the transport still holds is dropped.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: tests/io_test.cpp, containers_test.cpp, ring_buffer_test.cpp (model fuzz, SPSC and MPMC stress under TSan), frame_decoder_test.cpp (chunking equivalence, garbage, bad checksum/length, all framings), dispatcher_test.cpp (delegates, lookup, life cycle, concurrent dispatch and registration), link_test.cpp (loopback, garbage, full transport, ITransport adapter, unframed, sender/poller threads), checksum_test.cpp (CRC catalogue check values in both modes, custom Fletcher-16), lock_config_test.cpp (built with WIREFORGE_NO_STD_MUTEX). Each suite proves zero heap use with the allocation trap.

docs.title: Portability
docs.text:
The runtime and the generated code are verified on every combination of word size and byte order, with an x86 and an ARM target for little endian: quality/run_portability.sh cross compiles every test suite with the full warning set and runs it under qemu user emulation (docs/DECISIONS.md D34). The wire bytes of the golden frames are compared on every target.

Little endian Big endian 64-bit x86-64 (host), aarch64 s390x 32-bit i686, armhf (ARMv7) powerpc

The host is also built with plain char unsigned (cmake --preset unsigned-char, the ARM default) and with AddressSanitizer and UBSan (which includes the alignment check). The tests run under qemu-user, not on hardware. Conversions whose source width depends on the platform use narrow_to<T>(value) (bit_utils.hpp); counters accept any unsigned amount. The runtime uses atomics of at most the size of a pointer, so targets without 64-bit atomics (32-bit PowerPC, Cortex-M) need no libatomic.

docs.title: Environments
docs.text:
The runtime and the generated code use only the C++17 standard library (an allow list of headers, checked by quality/check_os_neutral.py) and test for no operating system. The CI proves it in these environments:

Environment Compiler What is proved Linux GCC 13, Clang 18 build, all tests, sanitizers Windows MSVC x64, MSVC x86, clang-cl build with /W4 /WX, all tests macOS (Apple silicon) AppleClang build, all tests Android NDK Clang, Bionic, libc++ (arm64-v8a, armeabi-v7a, x86_64) the runtime tests and the tests of the generated code build and link with the full warning set; they are not run, because a Bionic binary does not run on a glibc host FreeRTOS arm-none-eabi-gcc, newlib-nano, Cortex-M4F the generated self-tests of three examples and the runtime with several tasks run on QEMU mps2-an386

The generator, the command line and the server (Python) are tested on Linux, Windows and macOS.

On an RTOS the locking of the runtime is the lock of the kernel. tests/rtos/freertos_lock.hpp is a complete lock policy on a FreeRTOS mutex; the harness makes it the default lock of the library with -DWIREFORGE_NO_STD_MUTEX -DWIREFORGE_DEFAULT_LOCK=FreeRtosLock (see the table of config.hpp) and uses it for a ring and a link between tasks. The library allocates nothing, so a kernel that only allocates for its own objects is enough. quality/run_freertos.sh builds and runs the harness; quality/run_android.sh builds for the NDK.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
runtime/requirements.yaml holds the requirements of the runtime (RTR-<header>-NNN): the text, the header and the symbols that implement it (checked against the header), the kinds of generated low-level requirements it realizes and how it is verified (test, analysis or review). The file is written and reviewed by people; the first version was drafted from the Doxygen comments and the tests, so it describes the code and does not yet stand apart from it. Every unit test records the requirements it verifies as the first statement of its body (::testing::Test::RecordProperty("requirements", "RTR-...")); only the tests of the allocation trap, which check the test tooling, record none. Ids are never reused: a dropped requirement stays with retired: true.

Claims about several threads (the standard mutex lock, the single-producer ring, the locked ring, concurrent dispatch) have verification: analysis: the evidence is for single-threaded use with the null lock, and the rest is the integrator's to verify on the target. LoopbackTransport is a test helper and not part of that claim. array_access.hpp, expr_support.hpp, frame_layout.hpp and config.hpp have no requirement yet.

wireforge docs --runtime -o <dir> [--results <build>] [--strict] writes the dossier (requirements, design, tests, report, traceability, environment) of the runtime; quality/run_coverage.sh writes it to build/evidence-runtime and CI publishes it. A project's documents name the runtime requirements that realize their low-level requirements and the runtime version, and do not copy the dossier (docs/LIFECYCLE.md).

The coverage job of CI measures the runtime headers with the runtime tests and the tests of the generated code of the examples (the differential harness, the fuzz targets replayed with golden inputs mutated at every byte and cut at every length, and all read lengths of a link) and fails below the line coverage it states in ci.yml. Template instances are counted one by one, as gcovr reports them, so a Link or FrameDecoder instance that is only compiled lowers the figure. Gaps are closed with tests; there are no exclusions.

docs.title: Evidence (quality/run_evidence.sh, CI artifact evidence)
docs.text:
File Shows no_heap.md Every runtime header, every generated header of every example and profile, and the generated self-tests, compiled with -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti -DWIREFORGE_NO_STD_MUTEX at -O0 and -O2: the external symbols of each object. Anything outside a short allow list (compiler runtime, string functions; printing in self-tests) fails, so no object references operator new/delete, malloc/free, exception or RTTI support or threads. trace_<project>.md, .csv Every enum, checksum, type, message, field and interface: model source (file:line, the ICD row), C++ symbol, generated file:line, the high-level requirements (reqs) and derived low-level requirements (llrs) of the element, and the generated tests that verify them. A second table lists every low-level requirement with its parents and test count. Messages and interfaces without tests, LLRs without tests, LLRs verified by the runtime tests, requirements without model elements and derived LLRs are listed. icd_<project>.md Layout per profile: offsets, sizes, bit positions, frame sizes, link RAM. hashes.txt Model hash (sha256 of the definition content) of every project; the same hash is in the banner of every generated file, so generated code is tied to the exact model.

Generated code carries the trace inline as well: each struct is documented with Defined in <file>:<line> (<JSON pointer>) and each member with its file:line. In a project with a requirements catalog, every struct, enum, checksum and interface also lists Requirements: <HLR ids>; <LLR ids>, and every generated test records the LLR ids it verifies (RecordProperty("requirements", ...), docs/SCHEMA_SPEC.md section 17).

A user type's own encode/decode is outside the no-heap check's object-file inspection unless its header is compiled into an example the safety-evidence pipeline builds; this is the same "informative, not a conformance claim" boundary as the rest of this table, not a new exception.

docs.title: Independent expectations
docs.text: The expected result of most generated tests is computed by the reference codec, which reads the model the same way as the code generator does. A misreading would show in both, so the tests could not catch it. Requirement vectors are bytes and values you write from the ICD; the reference codec only confirms them at validation time, and the generated tests compare with your values. That is the common-mode argument for keeping the two sources apart (docs/LIFECYCLE.md).

docs.title: Coding-rule mapping
docs.text:
docs/CODING_RULES.md maps the concerns behind MISRA C++ and AUTOSAR C++14 to what enforces them here. It is a coverage map, not a conformance claim.

Bare-metal targets define WIREFORGE_NO_STD_MUTEX (or WIREFORGE_DEFAULT_LOCK); the generated Handler and the runtime ITransport have protected non-virtual destructors, so no deleting destructor (and no operator delete) is emitted.

docs.title: WireForge schema specification, schema_version: 1
docs.text: Machine-readable form: schema/project.schema.json (root file) and schema/fragment.schema.json (included files). This document is normative for behaviour that JSON Schema cannot express; the semantic rules in section 13 are enforced by wireforge validate. Working examples: examples/.

docs.title: 1. Files and layout
docs.text:
• A project is a directory with a root file project.yaml plus optional fragment files.
  • Root keys: schema_version, schema_minor, generator, project, version, description, namespace, include, defaults, user_includes, bundle (export only), and the definition sections below. project/version identify the user's own project and ICD set; schema_version/schema_minor/generator identify the file format (section 11).
  • include lists globs relative to the root file. Fragments contain only definition sections (defines, profiles, checksums, enums, types, messages, interfaces). Sections are merged; a name defined twice is an error (SR-1).
  • YAML 1.2 is used (on/off/yes/no stay strings; 0x.. integers allowed).
  • Names (identifier): [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*, must not be C++ keywords (SR-2).

docs.title: 2. Defaults and resolution
docs.text: Effective value for endian, bit_order, range_check of a message as used on an interface: message value, else interface value, else defaults, else built-in (big, msb_first, encode: true, decode: true). Endianness and bit order are message-level only; there is no per-field override. A message used on two interfaces with different effective endianness gets one codec instantiation per endianness.

docs.title: 3. Built-in types and wire widths
docs.text:
Type Wire width Notes bool 8 bits (1..8 with bits) 0 = false, nonzero decodes to true only when value is 1; other values are OutOfRange u8 u16 u32 u64 8/16/32/64 unsigned i8 i16 i32 i64 8/16/32/64 two's complement f32, f64 32/64 IEEE-754 binary32/binary64 only, bit pattern via memcpy; no scale/offset char 8 unsigned byte holding ASCII/Latin-1; arrays of char map to fixed strings enum name width of its underlying integer type decoded value must be one of the listed values (else OutOfRange when range check is on) struct name sum of its fields serialized inline, no padding, no alignment, no hidden bytes user type name declared size_bytes opaque; wire format is entirely the user's own encode/decode free functions (section 14b)

Multi-byte values are written byte by byte using the effective message endianness; no host layout is assumed.

docs.title: 4. Bit-fields
docs.text:
• bits: n (1..64) narrows a field to n bits. Consecutive bit-fields form a bit group; a struct whose fields all have bits is an inline bit group when used as a field.
  • Packing follows the message bit_order: msb_first fills each byte from bit 7 downwards, lsb_first from bit 0 upwards. Fields larger than 8 bits continue across bytes in the same direction; byte order of a multi-byte group follows the message endianness.
  • A bit group must total a multiple of 8 bits (SR-10). Use reserved: true fields to pad explicitly.
  • Signed bit-fields are two's complement of the declared width and sign-extended on decode.
  • occurs on a bit-field is not allowed in v1 (SR-11). min/max apply to the logical (decoded) value.

docs.title: 5. Field attributes
docs.text: name, type, description, units (documentation only), scale, offset, bits, min, max, default, const, reserved, occurs, checksum, role (header/trailer only), if, since, deprecated. - default: initial value of init(); fields without default are zero-initialized. Arrays accept a list. Enum defaults use the value name. A default must lie in [min, max] (SR-6). - min/max: numbers or expressions; checked on encode and/or decode per range_check. With range_check.decode: false, decoding succeeds and the caller can run validate(). - scale, offset: the physical value of a field is raw * scale + offset (defaults 1 and 0; scale is never 0). The wire, min, max, default and const stay raw values. The generated code adds physical_<Struct>_<field>() and set_physical_<Struct>_<field>(); the reference codec decodes the physical value as well. Allowed on plain integer and floating-point fields only (SR-24). - const: written as the declared value, decode fails with ConstMismatch on difference. - reserved: written as default (or 0), ignored on decode unless also const.

docs.title: 6. Occurrence model: optional fields and arrays
docs.text: occurs: {min, max, count | fill} unifies optional fields and arrays. - max (required): capacity, integer or expression; drives static storage. - count: expression giving the number present on the wire (a previous field, bool allowed as 0/1). Count 0 means the field is absent. The count field must precede the field (SR-7). - No count/fill: fixed array of exactly max elements (e.g. 3 on platformA, 5 on platformB). - fill: true: elements fill the remaining payload; allowed on the last field of a message only and requires a constant element size (SR-8). count and fill are mutually exclusive. - Optional field = occurs: {max: 1, count: hasX}. min defaults to 0; count outside [min, max] is CountExceedsMax. - C++ storage is count + static array (StaticVector-like). Nothing is allocated dynamically.

docs.title: 7. Expression language
docs.text: Used in min, max, occurs.*, buffers.*, frame_size, max_frame_size, checksum-independent sizes. - Literals: decimal, 0x hex, 0b binary, true/false. - Names: defines, earlier fields of the same message (by name), enum members as Enum.member. - Operators (C precedence): ?: || && | ^ & == != < <= > >= << >> + - * / % unary - ~ !. - Functions: defined(NAME), min(a,b), max(a,b), ceil_div(a,b), sizeof(Type) (bytes; fixed-size types only). - Arithmetic is 64-bit signed; booleans convert to 0/1; division by zero in a constant expression is an error. - Exact semantics (wireforge.expr, D20): any intermediate result outside the int64 range is an error; / truncates toward zero and % takes the sign of the dividend (C rules); shift counts must be 0..63 and the shifted value non-negative; &&, || and ?: short-circuit; literals with a leading zero (012) are rejected (no octal); ceil_div rounds toward positive infinity. Generated C++ widens every operand to std::int64_t and calls wireforge::expr::{min,max,ceil_div} (runtime/include/wireforge/expr_support.hpp); if: conditions are emitted verbatim as #if expressions. - if: conditions use the preprocessor subset: integers, defines, defined(), comparisons, && || !, parentheses. They must not reference fields.

docs.title: 8. Defines, profiles and conditional layout
docs.text:
• defines: named integer constants with default values. Generated headers emit defines::kNAME constants that take the value of the macro NAME when the build defines it (-DNAME=value) and the model default otherwise; in #if conditions a define is written (defined(NAME) ? NAME : default). The generator itself defines no macros.
  • profiles: named sets of defines (e.g. platformA). Profiles do not change the generated source; they tell tools which variants to analyze and test.
  • if: on a field, struct, message or interface-message entry emits a real #if in C++. The wire layout may differ per profile; each profile is analyzed separately.

docs.title: 9. Checksums
docs.text: checksums declares reusable algorithms: - {algo: crc32}: CRC-32/ISO-HDLC (poly 0x04C11DB7 reflected, init/xorout 0xFFFFFFFF, check 0xCBF43926). - {algo: crc, width, poly, init, refin, refout, xorout, check?}: parametric CRC (Rocksoft model). - {algo: custom, impl, include, size_bytes}: user type impl from header include satisfying the runtime checksum contract (wireforge/checksum.hpp, D16): static constexpr std::size_t kSize (= size_bytes, 1..8), a copyable State, static State init() noexcept, static void update(State&, wireforge::Span<const std::uint8_t>) noexcept, static std::uint64_t finalize(const State&) noexcept; checked with static_assert(wireforge::is_checksum_v<impl>). For generated C99 code a custom checksum also names c_impl, a C function uint64_t f(const uint8_t *data, size_t length) over the covered bytes, and c_include, the header that declares it (relative to an include directory). A user constant (user_includes.constants) used in an expression of generated C has a c spelling, a macro or an enumerator; without it the C code uses value when the constant has no profile_values. A header entry of user_includes.headers can name a c_path, the header the generated C code includes in place of path (it defines the macros the c spellings stand for). A field uses it with checksum: {use, covers}. covers is {from, to} (inclusive field range in the same struct) or {scope: preceding | payload | header_and_payload}; the latter two are for header/trailer fields. The field is computed on encode and verified on decode (ChecksumMismatch). Its width must equal the algorithm width (SR-12). Checksums are optional everywhere.

docs.title: 10. Interfaces
docs.text: An interface is one communication endpoint with a remote party (our_to_nodeA, nodeB_to_our, ...). - version (semver, required): ICD version; may be carried on the wire by a role: protocol_version header field. - direction: tx, rx, both. endian, bit_order, range_check: defaults for its messages. - header: none or {fields}. Header field roles: sync (const marker), message_id, payload_length, protocol_version, sequence. A header with message_id enables header-based dispatch. - header: none means raw dispatch: the interface carries exactly one message type, or none (raw bytes) (SR-14). - trailer: optional fields after the payload (typically a checksum). - framing: none (each transport read is one frame), fixed (frame_size), sync_length (header has sync and payload_length), length_prefixed (header has payload_length). Non-none kinds need max_frame_size (drives static buffer sizes). length_counts says what the length field covers (default payload). resync: true rescans after garbage or bad frames. - messages: names or {name, id?, if?, since?}; id overrides the message id on this interface. - buffers.rx_bytes/tx_bytes: optional circular/linear buffer sizes; default derived from max_frame_size. - allow_trailing_bytes: default false; leftover payload bytes give TrailingBytes. - trim_trailing_zeros: default false; every payload is sent without its trailing zero bytes (the first byte always stays) and the receiver reads the bytes it did not get as zeros (MAVLink 2). Needs messages of fixed size (SR-25); changing it is a breaking change.

docs.title: 11. Versioning and file identity
docs.text:
Key Meaning Written by schema_version (int) file-format major; any incompatible change bumps it tool, required in every file schema_minor (int, default 0) additive format changes inside a major (minor 1: requirements, reqs; minor 2: vectors) tool generator {name, version} WireForge release that wrote the file (informational) tool on save/export version (semver, root) the user's project / ICD set user interface.version (semver) one interface's ICD version, may travel on the wire user

Compatibility policy (wireforge.versioning, rule SR-19): - format major newer than the tool supports: error, only this problem is reported (content cannot be trusted); - format major older: error in normal loading; the file goes through wireforge import, which applies the registered migration chain (register_migration(from_major, step), one step per major, run in order, result stamped with the current format). A missing step is an error ("no migration path"); - same major, newer minor: error (the file uses features this tool does not know); - generator newer than the tool: warning only.

Before the first official release the format is unstable (0.x tool versions may change it without migrations). From the release on, format 1 is frozen and every later major ships migrations from all earlier majors, so old interface files stay importable. Generated C++ carries the format version, tool version and model hash in its banner.

Interface compatibility (python -m wireforge.compat OLD NEW [--interface NAME], D26) compares each interface per profile and classifies every difference: - breaking (requires a major bump): any wire layout change of a header, trailer or message field (type, bits, occurs, const, reserved, checksum, role), inserted/removed/reordered fields, changed min/max or enum values, message id, effective endian or bit order, framing kind/sizes/length_counts, direction, removed messages; fields appended to a message unless the old interface has allow_trailing_bytes: true; - compatible (minor): renamed fields, changed defaults, added messages, resync or allow_trailing_bytes changes, appended fields that old receivers ignore; - doc (patch): descriptions and units. The report fails when the new interface.version is not at least the required step above the old one.

docs.title: 12. Error model
docs.text: Codec calls return Status values (docs/contracts/runtime-error-codes.md). Validation messages produced by tools carry file, line and JSON pointer.

docs.title: 13. Semantic rules (beyond JSON Schema)
docs.text:
• SR-1 No duplicate names within a section across root and fragments.
  • SR-2 Names are not C++ keywords and do not collide after C++ mangling.
  • SR-3 Every type resolves to a builtin, enum, struct or user type; struct graphs are acyclic.
  • SR-4 Every checksum use, interface message, enum default and covers name resolves.
  • SR-5 Expressions parse; names resolve; if conditions reference no fields.
  • SR-6 default, const lie in [min, max] and fit the type/bit width; min <= max.
  • SR-7 Fields referenced by occurs.count precede the occurring field and are integer/bool.
  • SR-8 fill only on the last message field with constant element size; max is positive.
  • SR-9 Message ids are unique per interface (after overrides); ids fit the header id field.
  • SR-10 Every bit group totals a multiple of 8 bits; bits does not exceed the type width.
  • SR-11 occurs is not combined with bits.
  • SR-12 Checksum field width equals algorithm width; covers ranges are ordered and in the same struct.
  • SR-13 role is used only in header/trailer; payload_length and message_id appear at most once per header.
  • SR-14 Raw interfaces (header: none) have at most one message; sync_length requires sync + payload_length header fields, length_prefixed requires payload_length.
  • SR-15 Enum values are unique per enum and fit the underlying type.
  • SR-16 Each profile evaluates every expression and if without error, producing consistent layouts.
  • SR-17 The layout adds no bytes beyond declared fields (no implicit padding is ever generated).
  • SR-18 User constants: names unique and not colliding with defines or field names; profile_values name existing profiles; without value either every profile has a value or the constant is opaque: opaque constants may appear only in value ranges (min/max), never in anything that changes layout or buffer sizes (occurs, framing, buffers).
  • SR-19 Version stamps: every file passes the compatibility policy of section 11; fragments carry schema_version.
  • SR-20 User header paths and include directories are relative, without .. segments (portable builds); this also covers a user type's include.
  • SR-22 Requirement test vectors (section 18) are consistent: the message, interface and profile exist, the message is on the interface, expect.fields names fields that exist on the wire value, an encoding vector gives every field, and the reference codec agrees with the vector in every profile it applies to.
  • SR-23 A field of an enum type without default (and without const) needs an enum member with the value 0, because init() and the reference codec start every field at zero; a dynamic array starts empty and is exempt.
  • SR-24 scale and offset are allowed only on a plain integer or floating-point field: not on enums, bool, char, structs, arrays, reserved or constant fields, roles and checksums.
  • SR-25 An interface with trim_trailing_zeros does not use fixed framing, and every message it carries has a fixed wire size in every profile (no dynamic arrays or optional fields), because the receiver restores the trimmed zeros up to that size.
  • SR-21 Every id in a reqs list names an entry of the requirements catalog (section 17). An unused catalog entry is not an error.

Implementation notes (wireforge.validate, D21-D23): every issue carries [SR-n], file, line and JSON pointer. SR-10 also limits a bit group to 64 bits (D19) and checks pure bit-field types where they are used; SR-12 verifies the check value of parametric CRCs and limits custom checksums to 8 bytes; SR-16 also requires every message to fit frame_size/max_frame_size together with header and trailer (dynamic arrays at capacity) and sizes/buffers to be positive; SR-17 rejects if: on a field inside a bit group. The negative corpus is tests/python/semantic_cases.yaml. Run python -m wireforge.validate <project>.

docs.title: 14. User includes: the gateway to application code
docs.text:
user_includes (root file only) lets definitions use constants and headers that belong to the application. 

user_includes:
  include_dirs: [app/include]                 # added to include paths of generated build files
  headers:                                    # emitted as #include in the generated user prelude, in order
    - { path: app/limits.hpp, style: quote }  # quote | angle ; optional `if:` preprocessor condition
  constants:                                  # integer constants usable in any expression, by plain name
    APP_MAX_FRAME:
      cpp: app::kMaxFrameBytes                # how generated C++ spells it (constexpr, enumerator or macro)
      value: 128                              # what the tools use (analysis, docs, tests, reference codec)
      profile_values: { platformB: 192 }      # per-profile override
  prelude:                                    # verbatim C++ lines after the headers (e.g. extern declarations)
    - "extern const std::uint32_t kLinkSpeed;"
- Tool value vs real value. The generator never parses C++. value is what analysis uses; the generated user_prelude.hpp contains static_assert(static_cast<std::int64_t>(<cpp>) == <value>), so drift between model and application fails at compile time (per profile in the generated per-profile test builds). - Static memory needs compile-time constants. cpp must name a constexpr variable, enumerator or macro. A link-time extern const may only be declared through prelude for runtime checks, never as a capacity (SR-18). - Opaque constants (no value) are allowed in min/max: the check is emitted against the symbol, tools skip evaluation. - cpp accepts only qualified identifiers (no expressions); header paths forbid quotes, angle brackets and newlines. prelude lines are emitted verbatim, are not analysed, and are the user's responsibility under the zero-warning policy. - Every generated header includes the single generated user_prelude.hpp first.

docs.title: 14b. User types: opaque field types backed by application code
docs.text:
user_types (root or fragment) lets a field's type be a user-owned C++ type whose wire form WireForge never inspects — only its fixed size. 

user_types:
  Fixed16:
    cpp: app::Fixed16                           # fully qualified C++ type name
    size_bytes: 2                               # fixed, positive; same in every profile (not an expression)
    include: app/fixed16.hpp                    # optional; added to the generated user prelude
    style: quote                                # quote | angle, default quote
    description: "Q8.8 fixed-point sample"      # optional
- ADL contract, same as a generated struct. The user writes the type itself plus void encode(const T&, wireforge::Encoder&) noexcept and void decode(T&, wireforge::Decoder&) noexcept, found by ADL. WireForge generates only min_wire_size/max_wire_size (both equal to size_bytes, since the size never varies); it never generates encode/decode for a user type. T must be default-constructible. - Treated like a struct field everywhere else. occurs, arrays and nesting inside other types all work. Opaque: bits, an occurs.count target, a checksum field, and min/max/default/const are all rejected — already caught by the rules that reject every non-integer, non-bool field type (SR-6, SR-7, SR-10, checksum field typing), no new rules needed. - Python reference codec. A user-type field's value is raw bytes of exactly size_bytes; the default value is size_bytes zero bytes. The reference codec never interprets the type's semantics. - Generated tests. Per-field value assertions are not generated for a user-type field (its C++ value cannot be expressed as a literal); only decode Status and wire-byte equality are checked. - Wireshark dissector. Shown as raw hex (FT_BYTES); the dissector cannot run the user's C++, so the value is never decoded or checked.

docs.title: 15. Export and import
docs.text:
• wireforge export <project> -o bundle.yaml merges all fragments into one ordinary single-file project (no include), stamped with the current format, plus bundle: {content_hash, source_files}. The sha256 covers definition content only (not stamps, not key order). Export refuses projects with structural or semantic errors.
  • wireforge import <bundle> <dir> verifies the hash (mismatch is an error; --no-verify overrides), applies migrations for older formats, validates structure and unpacks into the standard layout (project.yaml, profiles/, types/, messages/, one file per interface), every file stamped. --single-file keeps one file. A non-empty destination is refused.
  • A bundle is itself a valid project and can be loaded directly. Comments are not preserved by export (canonical form).
  • Standard layout written by import: project.yaml (project keys, defines, checksums, user_includes, include), types/types.yaml (enums, types), profiles/profiles.yaml, messages/messages.yaml, interfaces/<name>.yaml. The hash is verified before migrations run (it covers the content the exporter wrote). API: wireforge.bundle.

docs.title: 16. Encoding rules shared by the reference codec and generated code
docs.text: wireforge.codec.ReferenceCodec (one instance per profile) is the executable form of these rules; generated C++ must produce the same bytes and statuses (golden vectors in tests/golden/, regenerated with python -m wireforge.golden <project> <file> [--plugins file.py]). - Fields are written in declaration order; fields whose if: is false in the profile do not exist. - const fields are written with their declared value; decoding another value is ConstMismatch. reserved fields are written as default (or zero) and accepted with any value on decode. - Occurrences: when count is a plain field name the encoder writes the element count into that field (the caller's value is ignored); other count expressions must equal the element count. Counts outside [min, max] are CountExceedsMax, checked before the range of the count field. Fixed arrays need exactly max elements; fixed char arrays are zero padded (decode strips trailing zeros). fill consumes the rest of the payload, which must be a multiple of the element size (InvalidLength). - Values that do not fit the type or bit width are always OutOfRange; min/max and enum membership are checked when range_check is on for that direction (opaque constants are checked only by generated code). A bool wire value other than 0 or 1 is OutOfRange. NaN is outside every min/max range. - Bit groups follow section 4 (one container per group, written with the message endian). - Checksums: preceding covers the struct bytes before the checksum field, {from, to} the bytes of that field range, payload/header_and_payload the frame parts; a mismatch is ChecksumMismatch.
