Custom algorithms need a plugin (Python) or the impl type (C++). - Frames: header, payload, trailer. message_id and payload_length header fields are filled by the encoder; a length that does not match the frame is InvalidLength; fixed framing needs exactly frame_size bytes (no padding is ever added) and every frame must fit max_frame_size. Decoding verifies the trailer checksum before looking up the id. - Leftover payload bytes are TrailingBytes unless the interface sets allow_trailing_bytes. - trim_trailing_zeros: the encoder leaves out the zero bytes at the end of the payload (the first byte always stays), so the length field and the checksum cover the bytes that are sent; the decoder extends a shorter payload with zeros to the size of the message before decoding it. A payload of the full size or longer is decoded as it is.

docs.title: 17. Requirements and traceability
docs.text:
The model can carry the user's high-level requirements (HLR) and tie model elements to them. WireForge derives the low-level requirements (LLR) from the model itself and links both to the generated tests.

requirements:                      # root or fragment; ids are unique across files (SR-1)
  HLR-SNS-004:
    text: The sensor link shall reject readings outside the sensor's calibrated range.
    source: ICD-SNS-001 §4.2       # optional, free text
    verification: test             # optional: test (default) | analysis | review
- An id starts with a letter, continues with letters, digits and _ . : -, and has at most 64 characters. - reqs: [ID, ...] (at least one id, no repeats) is accepted on a field, types entry, message, enum, checksum, user type, interface, its framing and an interface message given in object form. An unknown id is SR-21; a requirement that no element uses is allowed. Projects without requirements or reqs behave exactly as before. - The requirements section and the reqs lists are part of the model hash, so editing a requirement text changes the hash in the banner of the generated code. - A file that uses these keys needs format 1.1; an older WireForge rejects it (SR-19).

Low-level requirements are never stored. wireforge.llr.derive() writes down what the model implies; each has a key built from names only (SensorReading.temperature.RANGE) and the displayed id LLR-<key>:

Kind Derived for VALUES, ALGORITHM every enum, every checksum LAYOUT, SIZE, TRUNCATED, TRAILING every type (LAYOUT) and message (all four) DEFAULT, RANGE, ENUM, BITS, COUNT, CHARS, CONST, CHECKSUM a field with that attribute (<Owner>.<field>.<KIND>, <Interface>.header.<field>.<KIND> for frame fields); RANGE, ENUM and BITS only where range checking is on FRAME_ENCODE, FRAME_MAX, DISPATCH, RAW every interface FRAME_SYNC, FRAME_LENGTH, FRAME_RESYNC, DISPATCH_UNKNOWN an interface with a sync field, a length (field or framing), framing other than none, a message_id field FRAME_TRIM an interface with trim_trailing_zeros

The fields of a nested type belong to the type (Vec3.x.RANGE), not to each message that uses it. An LLR inherits the HLRs of the elements it comes from (its field, its struct, the enum or checksum it uses, the interface and its framing); one without any is derived. DISPATCH_UNKNOWN is verified by the runtime tests, not by the tests generated for a project.

Every generated test records the LLRs it verifies as its first statement (::testing::Test::RecordProperty("requirements", "LLR-...,LLR-...")), so gtest writes them into its XML result and wireforge trace reads them from the test sources. The static size assertions of the layout analyzer are tests too (TEST(<Message>, WireSize), TEST(Interface_<I>, WireSize)), so SIZE and FRAME_MAX have a test.

docs.title: 18b. What real protocols showed
docs.text: Published protocols were written from their specifications (protocols/, docs/GUIDE.md), with vectors taken from the examples of the specifications and compared with independent implementations (pymodbus, pyubx2; tests/python/test_independent.py, tests/python/test_ubx.py). They found: - A receiver must check the constants of the header and, on a link without a frame decoder (framing: none), the checksum itself. It does now: the generated receiver refuses a frame with a wrong constant (ConstMismatch) or CRC (ChecksumMismatch) before the handler sees it. - A serial frame ends at a silence, not at a length. framing: none is how a driver that delivers one frame per read is described. - A checksum that must not cover the sync characters of the frame (UBX) is a custom checksum that skips the first two bytes it is given: scope: header_and_payload starts at the first header field. - A length field that counts bytes after fields that follow it (the unit and function code of Modbus TCP) leaves no header-based dispatch by function code; such an interface carries one message. - A count in bytes (Modbus byte count) is written as an expression (count: "byteCount / 2"); the byte count stays a field that a vector names. Protocols whose checksum needs more than the data (for example a seed byte per message) are described with a custom checksum; that was not attempted.

docs.title: 18. Requirement test vectors
docs.text:
A vector is a test you write from the ICD: bytes, and what they must decode to (or what a value must encode to). It verifies high-level requirements directly, with an expected result that comes from you and not from the model.

vectors:                          # root or fragment
  reading_nominal:
    description: Nominal reading from ICD-SNS-001 example 3.   # optional
    interface: sensor_to_us       # given: the bytes are a frame; absent: they are a payload
    message: SensorReading
    profile: ground               # optional; absent: every profile (or the single configuration)
    direction: decode             # decode (default) | encode | both
    bytes: "A5 5A 01 01 00 17 ..."  # hex; spaces and underscores are ignored
    expect:
      fields: { sensorId: 3, state: ready, temperature: 21.5 }   # or: { status: OutOfRange }
    reqs: [HLR-SNS-004]           # required, at least one
- expect holds either fields or status; a status is a runtime status other than Ok. With fields the vector must decode without error; fields may be a subset. Values have the shape of the decoded message: enum member names, nested mappings, lists, strings for char arrays. Wire-only fields (constants, checksums, reserved, plain count fields) cannot be named. f32 values are rounded to 32 bits before they are compared; the comparison is exact. - direction: encode or both needs fields and a complete value (every field that is always present); the bytes must be exactly what the value encodes to. - A project is valid only when the reference codec agrees with every vector (SR-22), so a wrong vector or a wrong model is found before code is generated. The agreement does not move the oracle: the generated C++ test (hlr_vector_test.cpp) compares with the values written in the vector. Vectors that need a custom checksum are skipped with a warning when no plugin is given. - Vectors are separate from the golden vectors in tests/golden/, which the reference codec produces as a regression baseline.

docs.title: Server
docs.text: pip install -e ".[server]", then wireforge serve --workspace <dir> [--host 127.0.0.1] [--port 8000] [--token T]. Every subdirectory of the workspace with a project.yaml is a project; its id is the directory name. The OpenAPI document is served at /openapi.json (wireforge serve --workspace <dir> --openapi openapi.json writes it); the UI types are generated from it. Code: wireforge.server (storage.py, app.py).

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
• The files are the single source of truth and stay git-friendly: the server keeps no copy, every request reads the files, so edits made by hand, by git checkout or by the CLI are visible immediately.
  • Entry and value edits go through the service layer (wireforge.service): comments, styles and the canonical layout are kept, so GUI edits produce minimal diffs (docs/CLI.md).
  • Optimistic locking: every file has an ETag (sha256 of its bytes) and every project an ETag over all its files. File writes need If-Match: <file ETag> (* creates a new file); entry/value edits need If-Match: <project ETag>. A missing If-Match is 428, a stale one 412 (reload and retry). Writes of one project are serialized by a lock, so of several concurrent writers with the same ETag exactly one wins.
  • External changes: GET /api/projects/{id}/wait?etag=E&timeout=S long-polls until the project ETag differs from E (200 with the new ETags) or the timeout passes (304); clients reload the changed files.
  • Authentication: with --token T every /api route except /api/health needs Authorization: Bearer T (401 otherwise). With --oidc-issuer/--oidc-audience it needs a JWT of that issuer instead (signature from the issuer's JWKS, iss, aud, exp/nbf with 60 s skew; 401 otherwise, 503 when the issuer cannot be reached); the sub and email claims live only for the request and are never stored. The JWKS is cached in memory for --oidc-jwks-cache-seconds (default 3600). See Deployment and operation for the limits.

docs.title: Routes
docs.text:
Route Meaning CLI equivalent GET /api/projects, POST /api/projects list projects / create a project, empty or from a template ls, wireforge init GET /api/templates the templates and published protocols a new project can start from (kind) wireforge init --list GET /api/projects/{id} entries per section, files, ETags, validation result wireforge validate GET /api/projects/{id}/state, GET .../wait ETags; wait for a change - POST /api/projects/{id}/validate validation result wireforge validate GET/PUT /api/projects/{id}/files/{path} read/replace a file (text + ETag) editor GET/PUT/DELETE /api/projects/{id}/entries/{section}/{name} read/create-or-update/delete an entry wireforge get/upsert/remove GET/PUT/DELETE /api/projects/{id}/value?pointer=P read/set/delete any element wireforge get/set/remove GET /api/projects/{id}/generate[?tests=false][&language=c] zip of the generated C++ (or C99) code (see below) wireforge generate --tests [--language c] GET /api/projects/{id}/preview[?language=c] generated C++ (or C99) files as text (nothing written) wireforge generate [--language c] GET /api/projects/{id}/analyze?profile=P&export=markdown\|csv\|json layout report (data) and ICD export (text) wireforge analyze POST /api/projects/{id}/requirements/import take a baseline of high-level requirements (JSON with the base64 file; needs If-Match) wireforge reqs-import POST /api/projects/{id}/requirements/lock number the low-level requirements (needs If-Match) wireforge reqs-lock GET /api/projects/{id}/docs the requirements, design, test and traceability documents as a zip (?strict=true fails like wireforge docs --strict) wireforge docs GET /api/projects/{id}/wireshark the Wireshark Lua dissector plugin (<project>.lua) wireforge wireshark POST /api/compat {old, new, interfaces?} compatibility of two projects of the workspace wireforge compat POST /api/projects/{id}/encode {message, value, interface?, profile?} payload and frame as hex wireforge encode POST /api/projects/{id}/decode {hex, message? \| interface, profile?} decoded payload or frame wireforge decode GET /api/projects/{id}/history git commits that changed the project git log POST /api/projects/{id}/compat {revision, interfaces?} the project at a git revision vs the working copy wireforge compat

Edit bodies accept dry_run (return the diff, write nothing) and strict (refuse results with validation errors). Responses carry the service Result (ok, issues, data, text) plus the new etag.

docs.title: Downloaded code
docs.text:
The zip of generate is self-contained: <project>/include/<project>/ (generated headers, or with language=c the C99 sources and headers, and, unless tests=false, generated_tests/), <project>/runtime/include/wireforge/ (the runtime), <project>/model/ (the project definition with its user_includes directories) and a README. The CMake paths of the test project are relative inside the zip, so cmake -S include/<project>/generated_tests -B build && cmake --build build && ctest --test-dir build works after unpacking; quality/run_generated_tests.sh does exactly that for example 02.

Custom checksums: the reference codec (golden vectors, playground) loads the project's plugins/*.py file that defines PLUGINS. The server runs that Python code, so it must only serve workspaces whose content is trusted.

docs.title: Deployment and operation
docs.text:
The server is a team tool for a trusted network, not a hardened multi-tenant service. Before exposing it:

  • Bind address. wireforge serve listens on 127.0.0.1 by default. The Docker image listens on 0.0.0.0 without a token; anyone who reaches the port can read and change every project. Outside a single-user machine start it with a token: docker run -p 8000:8000 -v "$PWD/projects:/workspace" wireforge wireforge serve --workspace /workspace --host 0.0.0.0 --token "$WIREFORGE_TOKEN".
  • Shared token or OIDC, no roles. --token is a single bearer secret compared in constant time; rotate it by restarting the server with a new value. --oidc-issuer URL --oidc-audience A instead requires a JWT signed by that issuer (pip install "wireforge[server,oidc]"). The two options exclude each other. Either way there are no roles, per-project permissions or audit log (git history is the audit trail): every authenticated caller may read and write every project.
  • TLS. The server speaks plain HTTP. Put it behind a reverse proxy that terminates TLS and limits request sizes (imports and file writes carry whole documents).
  • Token in the UI URL. The web UI reads the token from ?token=<T>, so it can end up in browser history and proxy logs; prefer a proxy that adds the Authorization header, or treat the token as low value and rotate it.
  • What the API can write. File writes are limited to .yaml/.yml files inside a project directory (paths that leave it, including through symbolic links, are refused); include directories and headers must be relative without ... The API cannot create Python files.
  • Code that runs on the server. Custom checksum plugins (plugins/*.py) are imported by the reference codec (encode, decode, playground, golden vectors). They can only come from the file system, so whoever may write the workspace directory (volume, git checkout) may run code in the server process: give that access only to trusted people.
  • Code that runs in your build. A custom checksum's C++ implementation (impl, include) and user_includes headers are compiled into the generated code and its tests. Review them like any other source in the repository.
  • MCP server. wireforge mcp talks over stdio to one local client; run_tests configures, builds and runs the generated test project with the local toolchain. Point it only at trusted workspaces (docs/MCP.md).
  • Importers. Excel files are parsed with openpyxl; for files from outside the team, install defusedxml as openpyxl recommends.
  • Backups and history. The server keeps no state of its own and does not commit: the workspace directory is everything. Keep it in git and back it up like any repository.

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text:
React + TypeScript (strict), built with Vite (ui/). npm run dev serves it and proxies /api to wireforge serve on port 8000; npm run build writes ui/dist/. Pass ?token=<T> for a server started with --token.

The look is plain and token based (src/styles.css): one set of color variables with a light and a dark value, the system setting by default and the button at the right of the header to switch; the choice is kept in the browser (localStorage, src/theme.ts). The selected entry is highlighted in the list, and the main action of each editor (save, create, download) is the accent-coloured button.

docs.title: New project
docs.text: "New project" in the header opens a form: choose a template (telemetry, command or raw), give the project id and name, and the first working model appears, already valid, with its first message open in the editor. "Next steps" then lead to the Playground and to Generate until hidden or another project is chosen. An empty workspace opens this form directly. The advanced parts of the schema stay in the YAML files and the CLI; the form does not offer them.

docs.title: Struct editor
docs.text:
• Entries: the project's enums, types, messages, interfaces, profiles and checksums, with "New ..." buttons.
  • Field table of a type or message: name, type (builtins, enums, types), occurrence (single, optional 0..1, fixed array, counted array, fill payload) with capacity and count, bits, min, max, default, units, scale, offset, if condition, description, checksum (use) and covered scope; rows can be added, moved and removed. Message editors add the message id and the message's encoding settings: byte order, bit order and range checks on encode and decode, each either set or inherited from the project defaults.
  • Live validation: problems the server would reject anyway (names, bits, capacities, counts) are listed while typing and block saving; after saving, the server's validation issues of the whole project are shown.
  • C++ preview: the generated struct and its functions, from GET /api/projects/{id}/preview.
  • Checksums: built-in CRC-32 or a parametric CRC (width, polynomial, initial value).

docs.title: Enums and project settings
docs.text:
• Enum editor: name, underlying type (u8 to i64), description and members (name, value); "Add member" proposes the next value. Non-identifier names, duplicate names or values and non-integer values are listed and block saving.
  • Project settings (header button): project name, version, description, C++ namespace, the default byte order, bit order and range checks, and the project defines. Each root key is written separately through PUT/DELETE /api/projects/{id}/value?pointer=/<key>, so only changed keys reach the file; a cleared field removes its key.

docs.title: Keys an editor does not show
docs.text: Every editor owns a fixed set of keys and saves the loaded definition with only those replaced, so keys it does not show (if, since, bit_order of an interface, ...) are kept unchanged. The following are edited in the YAML files or through the CLI, not in the UI: - user_includes and constants, - custom checksum implementations (impl, include, size_bytes), - an explicit covered range of a checksum field (covers: {from, to}; the UI offers the scope names only), - if and since of whole entries.

docs.title: Interfaces, profiles, versions and tools
docs.text:
• Interface editor: version, description, direction, endian, header (or none: raw dispatch) and trailer fields with roles, constants and checksums, framing (kind, frame size, maximum frame size, length counts, resync), the message list with per-interface id overrides, buffer sizes, trailing-byte tolerance and trimmed payloads (trailing zeros not sent). A new interface of a project that keeps one interface per file gets its own file (interfaces/<name>.yaml).
  • Profile editor: description and define values.
  • Tools (tabs): C++ preview; Layout (offsets, sizes, bit positions and a byte bar per field of a message, link RAM per interface; per profile); Playground (encode a JSON value to payload/frame hex and decode hex, with interface and profile, using the reference codec); Versions (git history of the project directory and the compatibility of the working copy with any earlier commit); Generate (every generated file of the project in C++17 or C99, and "Download code and tests" in the same language: the zip of GET /api/projects/{id}/generate with the generated headers, the GoogleTest project, the runtime, the model and a README with the commands that build and run the tests).

Saving shows Saved <section>/<name>.; a save that finishes after the user moved to another entry does not change the selection.

Saving uses PUT /api/projects/{id}/entries/{section}/{name} with the last project ETag, so concurrent edits are detected (412) and files keep their comments and canonical layout.

docs.title: Types are generated, not written
docs.text: npm run gen:types writes src/generated/schema.ts from schema/project.schema.json (json-schema-to-typescript) and src/generated/api.ts from the server's OpenAPI document (openapi-typescript); npm run check:types fails when they are outdated. The editor's conversions between table rows and schema fields live in src/model.ts.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: npm test (Vitest, jsdom): unit tests of src/model.ts and an end-to-end test that starts a real wireforge serve on a temporary workspace (tests/server.setup.ts) and creates, through the UI, a checksum, a bit-field type and a message with a nested struct, an optional field, a counted array and a CRC field; the project then validates and the preview shows the generated struct. A second end-to-end test edits the three-interface example (interface framing and header field, a profile define, a new interface, playground round trip, layout bit map, compatibility with the committed baseline) and checks with git diff that exactly the edited lines changed. A third end-to-end test creates a project, sets its settings and defines, adds an enum and a message with its own encoding settings, and checks that message and interface keys the editors do not show survive a save. A fourth one shows the generated files of a new project and downloads its zip, in C++ and in C; an empty workspace opens the new project form. A new project opens its first message and its next steps. A unit test switches the theme and checks that the choice is kept. Gates: npm run typecheck, npm run lint (typescript-eslint strict type-checked, React hooks), npm run check:types, npm test, vite build (quality/run_all.sh, CI job ui).

docs.title: Wireshark dissector
docs.text:
wireforge wireshark <project> -o <file>.lua writes one self-contained Lua plugin that dissects every interface of the project in Wireshark and tshark. The plugin has two parts. The first is a data table generated from the model: every profile's header, trailer, framing and messages, with fields expanded, bit positions, ranges and checksums. The second is a fixed interpreter (codegen/wireforge/wireshark_runtime.lua) that decodes frames by the same rules as the reference codec (docs/SCHEMA_SPEC.md, section 16). Code: wireforge.wireshark.

The plugin is tested with Wireshark 3.6, 4.2 and 4.6, on Lua 5.2 and Lua 5.4.

docs.title: Install and bind
docs.text:
• Wireshark: copy the file into the personal Lua plugins folder, then restart Wireshark or reload Lua plugins (Ctrl+Shift+L). To find the folder, open Help > About Wireshark > Folders. On Linux it is ~/.local/lib/wireshark/plugins; on Windows it is %APPDATA%\Wireshark\plugins.
  • tshark: run tshark -X lua_script:<file>.lua ....
  • Binding: each interface is one protocol. Its filter name is <project>_<interface>, in lower case, with characters other than letters, digits and _ replaced by _. Bind it to traffic in one of two ways:
  • Set its preferences under Edit > Preferences > Protocols: UDP port, TCP port, or User DLT (USER0..USER15, for captures of serial links and other raw byte streams). On the command line: -o basic_telemetry_sensor_to_us.udp_port:5000.
  • Use Decode As (UDP or TCP port).
  • Profiles: in a project with profiles, the Profile preference selects the layout of the captured traffic (-o <protocol>.profile:platformB).

docs.title: What is shown
docs.text:
• Field tree: one tree per frame, with Header, the message and Trailer. Structs and arrays become subtrees; array elements are labelled [i]. Bit-fields show their bit mask; enums show the member name. Units are added to the label (temperature [degC]) and descriptions become the field's blurb.
  • Display filters:
  • message fields: <protocol>.<Message>.<path> (e.g. basic_telemetry_sensor_to_us.SensorReading.accel.x > 1.5);
  • header and trailer fields: <protocol>.header.<name>, <protocol>.trailer.<name>;
  • one message type: <protocol>.<Message>.
  • Frames: the framing of the interface splits the stream into frames:
  • none: one frame per packet;
  • fixed: frames of frame_size bytes;
  • length_prefixed and sync_length: frame size from the length field, as counted by length_counts.

With trim_trailing_zeros a payload shorter than its message is dissected after being extended with zeros: the fields refer to a separate Zero-extended payload data source, and the message item says how many zero bytes were not sent.

Over TCP, a frame split across segments is reassembled. A packet may also hold several frames. With resync: true, bytes before the next sync pattern are shown as Skipped bytes (warning [Resync]). - Text: char arrays are Latin-1 and shown as UTF-8; NUL bytes inside dynamic strings are shown as \0.

docs.title: Decode problems
docs.text:
Every problem is expert info whose text starts with the status the generated C++ deserialize and the reference codec return. The problems are: - [Truncated] - [OutOfRange] - [ConstMismatch] - [CountExceedsMax] - [ChecksumMismatch] - [InvalidLength] - [TrailingBytes] - [UnknownMessageId] - [InvalidState]

All of them have severity Error, so _ws.expert.severity == error finds bad frames. Unlike the codec, the dissector keeps going after a bad value, so one frame can show several problems. When range_check.decode is off for a message, a value outside its range is only a Note, the same as the codec, which accepts it.

docs.title: Checksums
docs.text:
CRCs (crc32 and parametric crc up to 64 bits) are verified, and a correct value is marked [correct].

A custom checksum is verified only when another Lua plugin provides it. Wireshark runs every plugin in its own environment, so the hook must be set on _G: 

_G.wireforge_checksums = _G.wireforge_checksums or {}
_G.wireforge_checksums["vendor::SumChecksum"] = function(bytes)  -- bytes: Lua string
  local sum = 0
  for i = 1, #bytes do sum = (sum + bytes:byte(i)) % 65536 end
  return sum
end
Without a hook the field gets a Note Checksum not verified. The MAVLink 2 model brings its hook (protocols/mavlink2/wireshark/mav2sum.lua); it reads the CRC_EXTRA bytes from the project's crc_extra.h, found from its own place in the project, so a message added to the model is verified too.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• There is no heuristic detection: bind a protocol by port, user DLT or Decode As.
  • Over UDP, a frame that does not fit the datagram is [Truncated]; frames are never reassembled across datagrams.
  • Wireshark 3.6 is the oldest version the plugin is tested with. Older versions are not tested.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
tests/python/test_wireshark.py checks the plugin against the reference codec in real tshark, for every example project and tests/python/wireshark/project.yaml. That project covers bit groups wider than 32 bits, 64-bit ranges, count expressions, CRC-64, fixed framing and frame-counted lengths. Each profile and interface is tested three ways: - Golden frames must show exactly the decoded values. - Every frame with one byte changed (three changes per byte), cut short or extended must be flagged exactly when the codec rejects it. With framing none, the codec's status must be among the reported problems. - Frames split over TCP segments, with garbage between frames on resync interfaces, must all be dissected.

quality/run_wireshark.sh runs the tests against tshark 3.6 (Ubuntu 22.04), 4.2 (24.04) and 4.6 (26.04, Lua 5.4). quality/fetch_tshark.sh <release> downloads each tshark from the signed Ubuntu archive without root and runs it with its own C library. Without tshark ($WIREFORGE_TSHARK, the PATH or build/tshark-jammy), the tshark tests are skipped; the CI job wireshark always runs them.

docs.text: WireForge exchanges files with your tools and keeps everything in git. There is no live integration.

Tools that scan files for requirement ids find them in these places. The convention is part of the interface: a change is a breaking change of WireForge.

docs.title: In generated C++
docs.text:
/// Requirements: HLR-SNS-001, HLR-SNS-004; LLR-SensorReading.LAYOUT, LLR-SensorReading.temperature.RANGE
High-level ids come first, then a semicolon, then the low-level ids (shown with your numbering when a lock file exists). The line wraps with /// at 100 columns. Regular expression:

Requirements:\s*([A-Za-z0-9_.:-]+(?:\s*[,;]\s*[A-Za-z0-9_.:-]+)*)
The comment appears on structs, enums, checksums and interfaces, and only in projects that define a requirements section.

docs.title: In generated tests
docs.text:
Every test starts with 

::testing::Test::RecordProperty("requirements", "LLR-SensorReading.LAYOUT,HLR-SNS-001");
GoogleTest writes it into its XML result as <property name="requirements" value="..."/>. The ids of requirement vectors are high-level ids; the others are low-level ids.

docs.title: In Markdown
docs.text: Each requirement, test and element has an anchor and shows the id in the same line: <a id="llr-sensorreading-layout"></a>LLR-SensorReading.LAYOUT. The anchor is the id in lower case with every character outside a-z0-9- replaced by -.

docs.title: Characters
docs.text: An id uses A-Z a-z 0-9 _ . : -. The format of llr_ids.lock cannot produce anything else.

docs.title: GitHub Actions
docs.text:
The action action.yml in the root of this repository runs wireforge ci on a project: it validates it, compares it with the base of the pull request (wire compatibility and the version bump each changed interface needs), builds and runs the generated tests, and shows one summary on the run. The same command runs anywhere (wireforge ci --help), so GitLab and a developer's machine give the same answer (docs/integration/gitlab_ci.yml).

name: wireforge
on: pull_request
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }          # the base revision must be readable
      - uses: oguzhankynk/wireforge@v0.4.1
        with:
          project: icd                    # directory with project.yaml
          # test: "true"                  # generate, build and run the tests
          # plugins: icd/plugins/sum.py   # custom checksum plugins
          # comment: "true"               # also comment on the pull request

docs.title: What the summary says
docs.text:
Check Meaning Validation the structural and semantic rules of docs/SCHEMA_SPEC.md Wire compatibility per interface: the version bump the change needs (none, patch, minor, major) against the bump made; red when the version is too low Tests the result line of the generated tests (and the coverage gate of the generated code)

The changes of each interface are listed (the first 20), so a reviewer sees what moved on the wire. A project that did not exist at the base is not compared; the summary says so.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Reproducible: without wireforge-version the action installs the WireForge it is part of, the ref you wrote after uses:. Pin that ref to a release tag or a commit.
  • Permissions: the check needs no secret. comment: "true" posts the summary as a comment and needs permissions: { pull-requests: write } for the job.
  • Build tools: the tests need CMake and a C++17 compiler, which the GitHub-hosted runners have. GoogleTest is downloaded by CMake the first time.
  • License: running the action is free, in commercial product repositories too. Validating a project, comparing it with earlier revisions and generating, building and running its tests in CI count as non-production use (LICENSE; the generated code and the runtime/ library are MIT, runtime/LICENSE).
  • Data: the action collects and sends nothing. Only with comment: "true" it posts the summary on the same pull request, with the GITHUB_TOKEN of your workflow.
  • Support: open an issue at https://github.com/oguzhankynk/wireforge/issues.
  • Exit code: the step fails when the validation, the compatibility or the tests fail, after the summary is written.

Verified against: not yet (pilot pending); the action is exercised by this repository's own checks only.

schema_version: 1

    file: "avionics_demo/interfaces/*.hpp"

docs.title: WireForge tutorial
docs.text:
This tutorial builds one thing from start to end: the MAVLink 2 link of a small drone. You start from the published MAVLink 2 model, add a message, generate C++ for it, run the tests that prove the code, use it in an application that talks to an independent MAVLink implementation (pymavlink), check every change in CI, look at the traffic in Wireshark and let an AI agent edit the model. The last chapters show the team server and the documents for teams with an assurance process.

The one-minute video shows the way the tutorial goes, from the model to a vehicle that talks to pymavlink.

The commands of the tutorial run in the continuous integration of WireForge (quality/run_tutorial.py), all but the ones that need a GUI, Wireshark or an AI agent, so what you read here works with the version it belongs to.

docs.title: Developer track
docs.text: Chapter You will Time 1. Install and the first project install WireForge, start from MAVLink 2, encode frames, run the generated tests 10 min 2. The web UI browse the model, add the VFR_HUD message, try frames in the Playground, download the code 15 min 3. Your own protocol turn an ICD table into a project, learn the parts of a model, import a whole MAVLink dialect 15 min 4. Use the code build a vehicle that sends MAVLink 2 over UDP and answers commands, in C++ and in C; check it with pymavlink and talk to ArduPilot's simulator 30 min 5. On a microcontroller run the same vehicle in C on a Cortex-M4 (in QEMU), MAVLink 2 over its UART 20 min 6. Tests see what the generated tests prove, measure coverage, read the results 10 min 7. Versions and CI tell a compatible change from a breaking one and check every pull request 10 min 8. Wireshark see the frames of your protocol, checksums included 10 min

docs.title: Advanced track
docs.text: Chapter You will Time 9. AI agents (MCP) let Claude or another agent edit the model safely 10 min 10. Team server run the web UI for a team, with a token or in Docker 10 min 11. Documents and evidence generate requirements, design, test and traceability documents 15 min

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 to 3.13 and pip.
  • A C++17 compiler, CMake 3.21 or newer and Ninja or Make (chapters 1, 4, 5 and 6 build code).
  • For chapter 4, Linux or macOS (the example uses POSIX sockets) and pip install pymavlink.
  • For chapter 5, the Arm GCC toolchain and QEMU (sudo apt install gcc-arm-none-eabi libnewlib-arm-none-eabi qemu-system-arm).
  • For chapter 8, Wireshark 3.6 or newer (or tshark).

Work in an empty directory; every chapter continues where the previous one stopped. If you lose your way, start again from chapter 1: it takes a minute.

MAVLink is a project of the Dronecode Foundation; WireForge is not affiliated with or endorsed by it.

docs.title: 1. Install and the first project
docs.text: What we will do: install WireForge, create a project from the published MAVLink 2 model, encode a few frames and run the tests WireForge generates for it.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
python -m pip install "wireforge[server,mcp]"
wireforge --version
server adds the web UI of chapter 2, mcp the agent server of chapter 9. Make a directory for the tutorial and work in it: 
mkdir wireforge-tutorial && cd wireforge-tutorial

docs.title: Start from MAVLink 2
docs.text:
wireforge init drone --protocol mavlink2
wireforge validate drone
drone/ is now a working project: project.yaml describes the MAVLink 2 frame and six messages of the common message set (HEARTBEAT, GPS_RAW_INT, ATTITUDE, GLOBAL_POSITION_INT, COMMAND_LONG, COMMAND_ACK). drone/README.md says where the model comes from, what it covers and how it was checked against pymavlink. wireforge init --list shows the other templates and protocols (Modbus, CRSF, J1939, UBX, MAVLink 1).

Open drone/project.yaml and look around. The header of the interface link is the MAVLink 2 header, field by field; trim_trailing_zeros: true says that MAVLink 2 leaves out the zero bytes at the end of a payload.

docs.title: Encode a frame
docs.text:
wireforge encode drone Heartbeat '{ type: 2, systemStatus: 4 }' --interface link
wireforge encode drone CommandAck '{ command: 400 }' --interface link
Each command prints a whole frame in hex. The first one is a HEARTBEAT of a quadrotor (type: 2) that is active (systemStatus: 4): 
fd09000000010100000000000000020000040386ca
fd is the MAVLink 2 start byte, 09 the payload length, then flags, sequence, system and component id, the three-byte message id (000000, HEARTBEAT), the payload and the checksum.

The second one shows MAVLink 2's trimming: 

fd0200000001014d00009001a058
COMMAND_ACK has ten payload bytes, but only the command (400 = 9001, little endian) is not zero, so the frame carries two payload bytes (02). A receiver reads the missing bytes as zeros. Without --interface you get the payload alone.

Decode it again:

wireforge decode drone fd0200000001014d00009001a058 --interface link
The answer names the message, every field (the eight that were not sent are 0), the header and the checksum.

docs.title: Look at the layout
docs.text:
wireforge analyze drone
The report lists every message with the offset and size of each field, and the frame and buffer sizes of the interface: everything a C programmer would otherwise count by hand.

docs.title: Generate the code and run its tests
docs.text:
wireforge test drone -o build/drone
This generates C++17 for the model (build/drone/drone/model.hpp and interfaces/link.hpp), plus a GoogleTest project that checks every message and frame against WireForge's reference codec, builds it and runs it. All tests pass. For C99 code instead, add --language c.

What happened: the model was validated, the code generated (no heap, no exceptions, no RTTI), and the tests were derived from the model itself, not written by hand. Chapter 6 shows what they prove.

More: User guide, command line, definition format.

If something goes wrong: wireforge test needs CMake and a C++ compiler on the PATH; the message says which tool is missing. wireforge validate reports every problem with file, line and JSON pointer.

Next: 2. The web UI

docs.title: 2. The web UI
docs.text: What we will do: open the project in the web UI, look at a message, add the VFR_HUD message (what a head-up display shows: speeds, altitude, heading), try frames in the Playground and download the generated code.

docs.title: Start the server
docs.text:
wireforge serve --workspace .
Open http://127.0.0.1:8000. Every directory of the workspace with a project.yaml is a project.

  1. Project: pick drone.
  2. Entries: the parts of the model (enums, types, messages, interfaces, profiles, checksums). Click Attitude.
  3. Fields: the fields of the message in the order they are sent, with type, occurrence, bits, limits, default, units and scaling.
  4. Tools: C++, Layout, Playground, Versions and Generate, for the selected project.
  5. C++ preview: the generated struct of the selected message and its functions.
  6. Theme: switches between the light and the dark theme.

The files stay the source of truth: whatever you save in the UI is written to drone/project.yaml in the same layout a hand edit has, so git diff shows exactly what changed.

docs.title: Add a message
docs.text:
VFR_HUD (message id 74) has six fields. In MAVLink order (the largest types first):

Field Type Units airspeed f32 m/s groundspeed f32 m/s alt f32 m climb f32 m/s heading i16 deg throttle u16 %

  1. Click New message under Messages.
  2. Name it VfrHud, set the message id to 74 and the description to What a head-up display shows (VFR_HUD).
  3. Fill the rows of the field table from the table above.
  4. Add field adds a row; add six. The editor checks names, types and limits while you type; problems are listed under the table and block saving.
  5. Click Save message.
  6. Open the interface link, click Add message, choose VfrHud and click Save interface.

The same from the terminal, if you prefer it (stop the server first, or use a second terminal):

wireforge upsert drone messages VfrHud '{ id: 74, description: "What a head-up display shows (VFR_HUD).", fields: [{ name: airspeed, type: f32, units: m/s }, { name: groundspeed, type: f32, units: m/s }, { name: alt, type: f32, units: m }, { name: climb, type: f32, units: m/s }, { name: heading, type: i16, units: deg }, { name: throttle, type: u16, units: "%" }] }'
wireforge set drone /interfaces/link/messages/- VfrHud

docs.title: The checksum byte of a new message
docs.text:
MAVLink adds one extra byte to the checksum of every frame, CRC_EXTRA, that depends on the message definition. The model keeps these bytes in one list, drone/app/include/mav2sum/crc_extra.h, which the generated C and C++ code and the Python reference use. Add the line for VFR_HUD above the marker line: 

    X(77U, 143U) /* COMMAND_ACK */ \
    X(74U, 20U)  /* VFR_HUD */ \
    /* add new messages above this line */
The value comes from the MAVLink definitions; pymavlink prints it with python -c "from pymavlink.dialects.v20 import common; print(common.MAVLink_vfr_hud_message.crc_extra)". For many messages at once, wireforge import-mavlink common.xml imports a whole dialect, with these bytes computed (see the import guide).

wireforge validate drone

docs.title: Try frames in the Playground
docs.text:
Open the Playground tab (4 in the first picture).

  1. Choose the message Attitude and the interface link.
  2. Enter the value { "timeBootMs": 1000, "roll": 0.5 } (fields you leave out keep their defaults).
  3. Click Encode.
  4. Decode turns the hex in the Hex box back into values.
  5. The result: the 28-byte payload and the frame. The frame is 20 bytes instead of 40, because the last five fields (pitch, yaw and the three angular speeds) are zero and are not sent.

Layout shows the offset, size and bit position of every field and the RAM a link needs. Versions compares the working copy with any earlier git commit (chapter 7).

docs.title: Download the code
docs.text:
1. Language: C++17 or C99.
  2. Download code and tests: a zip with the generated code, its GoogleTest project, the runtime, the model and a README with the commands that build and run the tests.
  3. File: every generated file of the project.
  4. The selected file.

More: Web UI, team server.

If something goes wrong: wireforge serve needs the server extra (pip install "wireforge[server]"). Port 8000 in use: --port 8080. A save that is refused shows the reason under the editor; the file was not changed.

Next: 3. Your own protocol

docs.title: 3. Your own protocol
docs.text: What we will do: turn an interface control document (ICD) table into a project, add an interface, and meet the parts of a model. This chapter makes a second project next to drone; chapter 4 continues with drone.

docs.title: From a table
docs.text:
Many teams keep their messages in a spreadsheet. WireForge reads such a table as CSV or Excel (and C headers and CAN databases, see the import guide). Save this table as sensor.csv:

cat > sensor.csv <<'CSV'
section,name,id,field,type,bits,occurs,count,min,max,default,units,description
type,Vec3,,x,f32,,,,,,0.0,m/s2,X axis
type,Vec3,,y,f32,,,,,,0.0,m/s2,Y axis
type,Vec3,,z,f32,,,,,,0.0,m/s2,Z axis
message,ImuSample,0x0110,sensorId,u8,,,,1,32,1,,Sensor number
message,ImuSample,,accel,Vec3,,,,,,,,Acceleration
message,ImuSample,,temperature,f32,,,,-40,125,20,degC,Die temperature
message,Heartbeat,0x0001,uptime,u32,,,,,,,s,Seconds since start
CSV
wireforge import-icd sensor.csv sensor --name sensor --namespace demo::sensor --endian little
Every row is one field of a type or message; min, max and default become checks and initial values of the generated code.

docs.title: Add an interface
docs.text:
A message alone has no frame. An interface says how messages travel: a header, a trailer and how frames are found in a byte stream. This one has a sync word, a message id and a length, and a CRC-32 at the end:

wireforge upsert sensor checksums crc '{ algo: crc32 }'
wireforge upsert sensor interfaces imu_link '{ version: "1.0.0", direction: rx, header: { fields: [{ name: sync, type: u16, const: 0xA55A, role: sync }, { name: msgId, type: u16, role: message_id }, { name: length, type: u8, role: payload_length }] }, trailer: { fields: [{ name: crc, type: u32, checksum: { use: crc, covers: { scope: header_and_payload } } }] }, framing: { kind: sync_length, max_frame_size: 64, resync: true }, messages: [ImuSample, Heartbeat] }'
wireforge validate sensor
wireforge encode sensor ImuSample '{ sensorId: 3, temperature: 21.5 }' --interface imu_link
resync: true lets a receiver find the next frame after garbage or a broken frame.

docs.title: A whole MAVLink dialect
docs.text:
MAVLink keeps its messages in XML files, the dialects: common.xml, ArduPilot's ardupilotmega.xml or your own. wireforge import-mavlink turns a dialect and the files it includes into a project with every message and enum, the fields in the order MAVLink sends them and the checksum byte of every message computed from its definition. pymavlink ships the dialects, so take them from there:

python -m pip install pymavlink
DIALECTS="$(python -c 'import os, pymavlink; print(os.path.dirname(pymavlink.__file__))')/dialects/v20"
wireforge import-mavlink "$DIALECTS/common.xml" mavlink --name mavlink
wireforge import-mavlink "$DIALECTS/ardupilotmega.xml" apm --name apm --message HEARTBEAT --message AHRS2
wireforge encode mavlink SysStatus '{ voltageBattery: 12600, batteryRemaining: 87 }' --interface link
mavlink/ has the 210 messages of common.xml; apm/ has only the two messages asked for (and the enums they use). Both have the frame of the drone project, so chapter 4 works with them the same way. Import the dialect again when it changes: the project follows it.

docs.title: The parts of a model
docs.text:
Part What it is Example types a struct used by messages Vec3 messages what is sent, with a message id ImuSample enums named values of an integer field FixType checksums CRCs or your own algorithm crc32, MAVLink's checksum interfaces header, trailer, framing and the messages of one link imu_link, link profiles platform variants: defines and conditional fields platformA

Fields can be bit-fields (bits: 3), arrays of fixed or counted size (occurs), optional, conditional on a profile (if:), scaled (scale: 1.0e-7 for degrees sent as integers) or constant. The wire format is always the one you describe: WireForge never adds bytes.

Look at the generated code of the new project:

wireforge generate sensor -o build/sensor

More: definition format, importers, examples.

If something goes wrong: import-icd reports the row of every problem. A message that does not fit max_frame_size is refused with the size it needs.

Next: 4. Use the code

docs.title: 4. Use the code
docs.text: What we will do: build a small vehicle that speaks MAVLink 2 over UDP with the code generated from drone, and check it with pymavlink, an independent MAVLink implementation. The vehicle sends HEARTBEAT, ATTITUDE and VFR_HUD and answers COMMAND_LONG with COMMAND_ACK.

docs.title: Get the example
docs.text:
The application is in the WireForge repository, examples/tutorial/drone_app/: three files, CMakeLists.txt, main.cpp and udp_transport.hpp, plus ground_station.py. Its C version and the firmware of chapter 5 are next to it. 

git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/oguzhankynk/wireforge.git wireforge-src


cp -r wireforge-src/examples/tutorial/drone_app wireforge-src/examples/tutorial/drone_app_c .

docs.title: Build it
docs.text:
cmake -S drone_app -B build/drone_app -DDRONE_PROJECT="$PWD/drone" -DWireForge_DIR="$(wireforge cmake-dir)"
cmake --build build/drone_app
find_package(WireForge) finds the CMake package that comes with WireForge, and one line in CMakeLists.txt generates the code from your model when CMake configures the build: 
wireforge_generate(drone_model PROJECT "${DRONE_PROJECT}")
target_link_libraries(drone_sim PRIVATE drone_model)
Change the model and build again: the code follows.

docs.title: Fly it
docs.text:
python -m pip install pymavlink
build/drone_app/drone_sim 6 & python drone_app/ground_station.py; wait
The vehicle sends for six seconds; the ground station waits for its HEARTBEAT, sends COMMAND_LONG 400 (arm), and checks that COMMAND_ACK, ATTITUDE and VFR_HUD arrive: 
ground station: HEARTBEAT from system 1, type 2
ground station: ATTITUDE {'time_boot_ms': 1000, 'roll': 0.168..., 'pitch': 0.054..., 'yaw': 0.0, ...}
ground station: VFR_HUD {'airspeed': 0.0, 'groundspeed': 0.0, 'heading': 10, 'throttle': 0, 'alt': 10.47..., ...}
vehicle: COMMAND_LONG 400 (param1 1), answering COMMAND_ACK
ground station: COMMAND_ACK {'command': 400, 'result': 0, 'progress': 0, ...}
ground station: all messages arrived
pymavlink was not written with WireForge, so this is a real interoperability check: the frames, the trimmed payloads and the checksums are the ones every MAVLink tool expects. Ground station software such as QGroundControl listens on the same UDP port 14550.

docs.title: How the code is used
docs.text:
The handler receives decoded messages. Every message of the model has a callback, so adding a message to the model asks you, at compile time, what the application does with it: 

namespace mav = drone::mavlink2;
namespace link = mav::link;

class Vehicle final : public link::Handler {
public:
    void onCommandLongReceived(const mav::CommandLong& command) noexcept override { /* ... */ }
    void onVfrHudReceived(const mav::VfrHud& /*message*/) noexcept override {}
    // ... one callback per message
};
The endpoint joins the frame decoder, the dispatcher and the handler; the link reads a transport and sends frames: 
UdpTransport transport(14551, 14550);
Vehicle vehicle;
link::Endpoint endpoint(vehicle);
link::Link<UdpTransport> channel(transport, endpoint.decoder(), endpoint.dispatcher());

mav::Attitude attitude{};
attitude.roll = 0.2F;
channel.send([&](wireforge::Span<std::uint8_t> buffer, std::size_t& size) {
    return link::encode_frame(attitude, buffer, size, header);
});
channel.poll();  // reads what arrived and calls the handler
A transport is any class with a non-blocking send and receive (udp_transport.hpp is 60 lines); on a microcontroller it is a UART or a CAN driver. Nothing allocates memory, nothing throws, and trimming the trailing zeros of MAVLink 2 is done by the generated code: the application never sees it.

docs.title: The same in C
docs.text:
drone_app_c/ is the same vehicle in C99. One option of wireforge_generate makes the generated code C, and the library becomes a static library of the generated sources: 

wireforge_generate(drone_model PROJECT "${DRONE_PROJECT}" LANGUAGE c)


cmake -S drone_app_c -B build/drone_app_c -DDRONE_PROJECT="$PWD/drone" -DWireForge_DIR="$(wireforge cmake-dir)"
cmake --build build/drone_app_c
build/drone_app_c/drone_sim_c 6 & python drone_app/ground_station.py; wait
The ground station sees the same messages. In C the handler is a struct of callbacks, and a callback left NULL means "decode and ignore", so the vehicle sets only the two it acts on: 
self->handler.context = self;
self->handler.on_Heartbeat_received = on_heartbeat;
self->handler.on_CommandLong_received = on_command_long;
drone_mavlink2_link_link_init(&self->link, transport, &self->handler);
The vehicle itself (vehicle.c) knows nothing about UDP: main.c gives it a transport and calls vehicle_tick() every 10 ms. That is what lets the next chapter run it on a microcontroller.

docs.title: Against ArduPilot
docs.text:
So far both ends were ours. ArduPilot's simulator (SITL) runs the real ArduCopter firmware on your computer, and ardupilot_gcs/ is a small ground station in C for it, built from the import of the whole ardupilotmega.xml (every message of chapter 3's dialect, not just two). Get a SITL build of ArduCopter for Linux from ArduPilot's firmware server and its default parameters, and start it; it waits for a ground station on TCP port 5760: 

curl -fLO https://firmware.ardupilot.org/Copter/stable/SITL_x86_64_linux_gnu/arducopter && chmod +x arducopter
curl -fLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ArduPilot/ardupilot/master/Tools/autotest/default_params/copter.parm
./arducopter --model quad --defaults copter.parm -I0 &
Then import the dialect, build the ground station and run it: 
cp -r wireforge-src/examples/tutorial/ardupilot_gcs .
wireforge import-mavlink "$DIALECTS/ardupilotmega.xml" ardupilot --name ardupilot
cmake -S ardupilot_gcs -B build/ardupilot_gcs -DARDUPILOT_PROJECT="$PWD/ardupilot" -DWireForge_DIR="$(wireforge cmake-dir)"
cmake --build build/ardupilot_gcs
build/ardupilot_gcs/ardupilot_gcs 15
It sends a HEARTBEAT every second, asks for the telemetry streams, the AUTOPILOT_VERSION (with a COMMAND_LONG) and the parameter list, and counts what the autopilot sends back. With ArduCopter 4.7.2: 
ardupilot_gcs: 2992 frames decoded, 0 rejected
ardupilot_gcs: HEARTBEAT 15 (type 2), ATTITUDE 59 (roll 0.001), GLOBAL_POSITION_INT 59, VFR_HUD 59 (alt 584.08)
ardupilot_gcs: AUTOPILOT_VERSION 1 (firmware 4.7.2), COMMAND_ACK 1 (command 512, result 0)
ardupilot_gcs: PARAM_VALUE 1369 of 1369
Every frame of the autopilot, of more than thirty kinds, is decoded and its checksum verified; none is rejected. The handler has callbacks for seven messages, and the others are decoded and ignored. Stop the simulator with kill %1.

More: generated code (C++ and C), runtime, examples/cmake_consumer/.

If something goes wrong: Could not find a package configuration file provided by "WireForge": pass -DWireForge_DIR="$(wireforge cmake-dir)". Port 14550 or 14551 in use: another ground station or simulator is running.

Next: 5. On a microcontroller

docs.title: 5. On a microcontroller
docs.text: What we will do: run the C vehicle of chapter 4 as firmware on an Arm Cortex-M4, with MAVLink 2 over the microcontroller's UART, and fly it against the same pymavlink ground station. No board is needed: QEMU emulates Arm's MPS2 board (mps2-an386, a Cortex-M4 with a CMSDK UART) and connects its UART to a TCP port.

docs.title: The tools
docs.text:
The Arm GCC toolchain with newlib, and QEMU. On Debian or Ubuntu: 

sudo apt install gcc-arm-none-eabi libnewlib-arm-none-eabi qemu-system-arm
(macOS: brew install --cask gcc-arm-embedded and brew install qemu.)

docs.title: Build the firmware
docs.text:
cp -r wireforge-src/examples/tutorial/drone_firmware .
cmake -S drone_firmware -B build/drone_firmware -DDRONE_PROJECT="$PWD/drone" -DWireForge_DIR="$(wireforge cmake-dir)" \
  -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE="$PWD/wireforge-src/cmake/toolchains/arm-none-eabi.cmake"
cmake --build build/drone_firmware
arm-none-eabi-size build/drone_firmware/drone_firmware.elf
The firmware is the generated C code of drone, vehicle.c of chapter 4 unchanged, and two small files of its own: main.c (the UART and the timer) and startup.c (what runs before main). It needs about 22 KB of flash and 14 KB of RAM (text and bss). Of the flash, the generated code, the runtime and the vehicle are about 12 KB and the C library's snprintf and sinf about 6 KB; the RAM is mostly the stack and the link buffers, sized for the largest MAVLink frame. Nothing is allocated at run time.

docs.title: Fly it
docs.text:
qemu-system-arm -M mps2-an386 -cpu cortex-m4 -display none -semihosting-config enable=on,target=native \
  -serial tcp:127.0.0.1:5760,server=on,wait=off -kernel build/drone_firmware/drone_firmware.elf &
sleep 1
python drone_app/ground_station.py tcp:127.0.0.1:5760
kill %1
QEMU runs the firmware and offers the board's UART on TCP port 5760; the ground station connects to it instead of listening on UDP: 
firmware: MAVLink 2 on UART0
ground station: HEARTBEAT from system 1, type 2
ground station: ATTITUDE {'time_boot_ms': 2000, 'roll': 0.18..., 'pitch': -0.04..., ...}
ground station: VFR_HUD {'airspeed': 0.0, 'groundspeed': 0.0, 'heading': 20, ...}
vehicle: COMMAND_LONG 400 (param1 1), answering COMMAND_ACK
ground station: COMMAND_ACK {'command': 400, 'result': 0, ...}
ground station: all messages arrived
The lines of the firmware reach the terminal through semihosting, the debugger channel QEMU emulates.

docs.title: How the firmware works
docs.text:
The transport is the UART: bytes go out as long as the UART takes them, and received bytes are read until it is empty. Neither function blocks on input, so the link never waits for the other side: 

static size_t uart_receive(void* context, uint8_t* buffer, size_t capacity) {
    size_t got = 0U;
    (void)context;
    while (got < capacity && (UART_STATE & UART_RX_FULL) != 0U) {
        buffer[got++] = (uint8_t)UART_DATA;
    }
    return got;
}
There is no operating system: main sets up the UART and the SysTick timer and calls vehicle_tick() every time the timer has counted 10 ms. startup.c copies the initialized data, clears the rest and switches on the floating-point unit (the code is built for it), as every Cortex-M4 start-up does.

docs.title: On your board
docs.text:
• The UART: replace the four register macros and uart_send/uart_receive with your board's UART (or its HAL calls). With interrupts, let the receive interrupt put bytes into a ring buffer (wf_ring of the runtime) and let uart_receive take them from there.
  • The clock: CPU_HZ is the clock of the SysTick timer; any 10 ms tick works, from a timer interrupt as well.
  • With an RTOS: call vehicle_tick() from one task every 10 ms. The C runtime has no locks, so the link belongs to that task; the C++ runtime has a lock policy for kernel mutexes (the FreeRTOS example is in tests/rtos).
  • Less memory: the formatted printing of on_command_long and the sine of the simulated attitude bring in about 6 KB of the C library; real firmware reads its sensors instead. The link buffers follow max_frame_size of the interface.

More: C runtime, generated C code, runtime environments.

If something goes wrong: arm-none-eabi-gcc not found: install the toolchain or put it on the PATH. Connection refused from the ground station: QEMU is not running (look at its message) or port 5760 is taken. QEMU stops at once with exit code 2: the firmware hit a fault; on a board of your own, check the start-up code first.

Next: 6. Tests

docs.title: 6. Tests
docs.text: What we will do: look at the tests WireForge generated for drone, measure the coverage of the generated code and read the results.

docs.title: What is tested
docs.text:
wireforge test drone -o build/drone
ls build/drone/drone/generated_tests
| File | What it checks | |------|----------------| | message_test.cpp | per message: defaults, round trips of values the generator picks, limits, every decode error | | golden_test.cpp | golden frames from the reference codec: encode_frame gives the same bytes, decoding gives the same values | | interface_test.cpp | per interface: dispatch of every message, byte-by-byte delivery, garbage before a frame, broken frames, trimmed frames | | diff_harness.cpp | a differential test: random values and frames through the generated code and the reference codec | | fuzz_target.cpp | a libFuzzer target over the decoder (-DWIREFORGE_FUZZ=ON with Clang) | | selftest.cpp | a self-test without a framework, heap or exceptions, for embedded targets |

Every expectation comes from WireForge's reference codec, an independent Python implementation of the encoding rules, not from the generated code itself. For MAVLink 2 the reference codec in turn is checked against pymavlink.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
python -m pip install gcovr
wireforge test drone -o build/drone --coverage
The coverage build fails unless every line, branch and function of the generated code is run by the tests (100 %). The generated code has no branch of its own that a test cannot reach, so the gate holds for any model.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
The coverage build writes results/ next to the build: the JUnit XML of the tests and the coverage reports. Each test records the requirements it verifies, which chapter 11 turns into a traceability matrix: 

TEST(Interface_link, TrimsTrailingZeros) {
    ::testing::Test::RecordProperty("requirements", "LLR-link.FRAME_TRIM");

More: generated test project, quality policy.

If something goes wrong: --coverage needs gcovr and GCC or Clang. A failing generated test is a defect of WireForge (the model was valid); please report it with the model.

Next: 7. Versions and CI

docs.title: 7. Versions and CI
docs.text: What we will do: let WireForge tell a compatible change from a breaking one, and check every pull request.

docs.title: Compare two versions
docs.text:
Keep a copy of the model as it is, then change a description:

cp -r drone drone-1.0
wireforge set drone /messages/VfrHud/description "Speeds, altitude and heading for a head-up display (VFR_HUD)."
wireforge compat drone-1.0 drone || echo "the version must change"
compat lists the change (doc: documentation only) and fails: every change of an interface needs a new version, here a patch version. Give it one:

wireforge set drone /interfaces/link/version 1.0.1
wireforge compat drone-1.0 drone
Now a change on the wire:

wireforge set drone /messages/VfrHud/fields/5/type u8
wireforge compat drone-1.0 drone || echo "breaking, as expected"
throttle is now one byte instead of two: every receiver of version 1.0 would read VFR_HUD wrongly. compat calls it a breaking change that needs a new major version (2.0.0). Adding a message would be a compatible change (a minor version), because receivers that do not know it report it as an unknown id and go on. Undo the breaking change:

wireforge set drone /messages/VfrHud/fields/5/type u16
wireforge compat drone-1.0 drone

docs.title: In git
docs.text:
wireforge ci does the same against a git revision, validates, and can build and run the generated tests (--test):

git init -q && git add drone && git -c user.name=me -c user.email=me@example.com commit -qm "drone 1.0.1"
wireforge set drone /messages/Heartbeat/description "Who is there and in which state (HEARTBEAT, 1 Hz)."
wireforge set drone /interfaces/link/version 1.0.2
wireforge ci drone --base HEAD
It prints the summary a pull request would get, in Markdown.

docs.title: On every pull request
docs.text:
The WireForge repository is also a GitHub Action. In .github/workflows/wireforge.yml: 

name: wireforge
on: pull_request
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }          # the base revision must be readable
      - uses: oguzhankynk/wireforge@v0.4.1
        with:
          project: drone
          test: "true"                    # generate, build and run the tests
The run shows one summary: validation, the version bump every changed interface needs and the result of the tests. Running it in CI is free, also in commercial repositories. For GitLab there is an example job in the repository.

More: GitHub Actions, compatibility rules.

Next: 8. Wireshark

docs.title: 8. Wireshark
docs.text: What we will do: generate a Wireshark dissector for drone and look at the vehicle's traffic.

docs.title: The dissector
docs.text:
wireforge wireshark drone -o drone.lua
drone.lua is a Lua plugin for Wireshark 3.6 or newer, and drone/wireshark/mav2sum.lua the hook that verifies MAVLink's checksum, with the CRC_EXTRA byte of every message (VFR_HUD's too: the hook reads the project's crc_extra.h). Start Wireshark with both: 
wireshark -X lua_script:drone.lua -X lua_script:drone/wireshark/mav2sum.lua
To load them at every start instead, copy them into your personal plugin directory (Wireshark shows it under Help > About Wireshark > Folders), with drone/app/include/mav2sum/crc_extra.h next to the hook.

docs.title: Look at the traffic
docs.text:
Start a capture on the loopback interface with the filter udp port 14550, run the vehicle and the ground station of chapter 4 again, and tell Wireshark that UDP port 14550 carries drone_link: Analyze > Decode As, or the protocol preference UDP port.

Every frame becomes a tree. Here is a VFR_HUD frame of the vehicle:

  1. The protocol item names the project, the interface with its version, and the message.
  2. The header: every field of the model, and the bits of componentId and messageId, which share one 32-bit group.
  3. The message, with units. A frame whose trailing zeros were not sent is dissected as the whole message, and the item says how many zero bytes were left out.
  4. The checksum, verified by the hook with the message's CRC_EXTRA byte. Display filters use the field names of the model: 
    drone_link.VfrHud.alt > 10
drone_link.header.sequence == 42
    A broken frame is marked with the status the generated decoder returns ([ChecksumMismatch], [InvalidLength], ...).

Without the GUI, tshark shows the same: 

tshark -i lo -f "udp port 14550" -X lua_script:drone.lua -X lua_script:drone/wireshark/mav2sum.lua -o drone_link.udp_port:14550 -V

More: Wireshark dissector.

If something goes wrong: no drone_link in the packet list: the port preference is not set. Checksum not verified: the hook mav2sum.lua is not loaded.

Next: 9. AI agents (MCP)

docs.title: 9. AI agents (MCP)
docs.text: What we will do: connect an AI agent to the workspace through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), so that it can read, change, validate and test the model with the same rules as the command line.

docs.title: Connect
docs.text:
wireforge mcp --workspace <dir> serves MCP on standard input and output. With Claude Code, in the tutorial directory: 

claude mcp add wireforge -- wireforge mcp --workspace "$PWD"
Other MCP clients (Claude Desktop, IDE assistants) take the same command in their configuration: 
{ "mcpServers": { "wireforge": { "command": "wireforge", "args": ["mcp", "--workspace", "/path/to/wireforge-tutorial"] } } }


wireforge mcp --help

docs.title: Ask
docs.text:
Some requests that work well: - "List the messages of drone and their sizes." - "Add MAVLink's SYS_STATUS message to drone: these are its fields ... Show me the diff before you write it." - "Encode a VFR_HUD frame with alt 12.5 and decode it again." - "Make throttle of VfrHud a u8 and tell me what that breaks." - "Generate the code and run the tests of drone."

The agent works through tools such as list_messages, upsert_struct, validate_project, encode_sample, compat_check, generate_code and run_tests. Every write can be a dry run that returns the diff first, every write is validated, and the files keep their canonical layout, so the change you review in git is exactly what the agent did.

Good to know: the agent edits the model, not the generated code, and WireForge checks every result, so a wrong field size is a validation error or a failing compatibility check, not a silent bug. For a new MAVLink message, ask the agent to add its CRC_EXTRA line too (chapter 2).

More: MCP server.

Next: 10. Team server

docs.title: 10. Team server
docs.text: What we will do: run the web UI for a team.

docs.title: With a token
docs.text:
wireforge serve --workspace . --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --token "$(openssl rand -hex 16)"
Open http://<host>:8000/?token=<the token>. Every request needs the token; without --token anyone who reaches the port can change the models. For single sign-on, --oidc-issuer checks the tokens of your identity provider instead.

Several people can edit the same project: every save carries the version of the project it was based on, and a save over a newer version is refused instead of overwriting someone else's work. The Versions tab compares the working copy with the git history.

docs.title: In Docker
docs.text:
The repository has a Dockerfile with WireForge, the web UI and the compilers: 

docker build -t wireforge https://github.com/oguzhankynk/wireforge.git
docker run -p 8000:8000 -v "$PWD:/workspace" wireforge

The server is meant for a team's internal network. Read the deployment notes before you expose it.

More: server and REST API, deployment and operation.

Next: 11. Documents and evidence

docs.title: 11. Documents and evidence
docs.text: What we will do: turn the model, the generated tests and their results into requirements, design, test and traceability documents. This is for teams that work with a development or assurance process; nothing in chapters 1 to 10 needs it.

docs.title: Requirements in the model
docs.text: The MAVLink 2 model already has high-level requirements: requirements: in drone/project.yaml (MAV2-001 to MAV2-005), and elements point at them with reqs:. WireForge derives the low-level requirements from the model itself (the layout of every message, the range of every field, the trimming of the interface, ...) and the generated tests record which ones they verify.

docs.title: Documents
docs.text:
wireforge test drone -o build/drone-evidence --coverage
wireforge docs drone -o build/docs --results build/drone-evidence/drone/generated_tests/build/coverage
ls build/docs
build/docs holds Markdown documents (and CSV): the requirements, the design of every message and interface, the test procedures and their results, and a traceability matrix from each high-level requirement through the low-level requirements and the generated code to the tests that verify it, with their result and the coverage. --export reqif writes ReqIF for requirement tools such as DOORS Next or Polarion.

wireforge trace drone --format csv -o build/trace.csv

docs.title: What this is and is not
docs.text:
The documents support a process such as DO-178C, ISO 26262 or IEC 61508 and the assessment of WireForge as a tool in it. They do not by themselves give conformity, certification or tool qualification; those depend on your whole project and its assessor.

More: lifecycle documents, DO-178C, tool integrations.

That is the end of the tutorial. The user guide and the reference documents go on from here.
